questions.title: Why Syndrome Extraction Never Reveals the Encoded Data
questions.prompt: In the 3-qubit bit-flip code, syndrome extraction uses an ancilla qubit entangled to two data qubits via CNOTs, then measured, to get the Z1Z2 (or Z2Z3) syndrome bit. Explain precisely why this measurement can tell you whether an X error occurred without ever revealing the encoded amplitudes α and β of α|000⟩+β|111⟩, and connect this explicitly to why it does not violate the no-cloning theorem.
questions.modelAnswer: The ancilla picks up only a relationship fact, never an amplitude fact. Z1Z2 commutes with both logical basis states |000⟩ and |111⟩ with the identical +1 eigenvalue, regardless of which logical state (or superposition of both) is actually encoded. Because the measurement outcome is the same +1 for either basis state, measuring Z1Z2 cannot distinguish 'is this closer to logical |0⟩ or logical |1⟩,' so it cannot collapse or reveal anything about the superposition coefficients α and β. What it can detect is whether an error has disturbed the normal agreement pattern between qubits 1 and 2 — a strictly binary fact about relative value, not about which logical state is present. The CNOT-ancilla circuit extracts exactly that one bit (agree/disagree) and nothing more. Because no step of this process ever copies or exposes α or β, no-cloning is never at risk — no-cloning forbids copying an unknown quantum state, and this circuit never attempts to copy the data qubits' state onto the ancilla; it only entangles the ancilla to a parity relationship among them, then destructively measures the ancilla alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as a parity check, not a readout. The ancilla only ever learns 'did qubits 1 and 2 agree,' and that answer comes out the same whether the logical qubit is 0, 1, or any superposition, because both |000⟩ and |111⟩ give the same +1 eigenvalue under Z1Z2. Since the measurement result doesn't depend on which logical state is encoded, it can't be used to infer it — that's the whole trick. And because nothing about the actual superposition is ever copied anywhere, no-cloning stays completely intact; this is a non-destructive measurement of an error syndrome, not a measurement of the protected information.
questions.example: Encode |ψ⟩=0.6|0⟩+0.8|1⟩ as 0.6|000⟩+0.8|111⟩. Measuring Z1Z2 on this exact superposition (no error) gives +1 with certainty, exactly as it would for a pure |000⟩ or pure |111⟩ state — the measurement result carries no information about the 0.6/0.8 split.
commonMistakes: Assuming any measurement touching the data qubits must reveal the encoded amplitudes
Confusing 'entangling an ancilla to data qubits' with 'cloning the data qubits' state'
Missing that both logical basis states share the same eigenvalue under the stabilizer, which is what hides the logical information
Thinking the syndrome gives a probabilistic hint about α and β rather than zero information
keyPoints: Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 give the same eigenvalue (+1) for both |000⟩ and |111⟩
Syndrome measurement reveals only a relationship (agreement/disagreement), never an amplitude
No-cloning is not violated because nothing about α, β is ever copied
This is a non-destructive measurement with respect to the protected logical superposition

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why Z1Z2 cannot distinguish logical |0⟩ from |1⟩
Correctly identifies the syndrome as a relationship/parity fact, not an amplitude fact
Connects the explanation explicitly to no-cloning
Clear, technically accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Deriving a Syndrome From the Stabilizer Anticommutation Rule
questions.prompt: Using the stabilizer formalism's commutation rule (a Pauli error E is detected by stabilizer S exactly when they anticommute), derive the syndrome for an X error on qubit 2 of the 3-qubit bit-flip code, whose stabilizers are Z1Z2 and Z2Z3. Show your reasoning for each stabilizer separately, and state the resulting 2-bit syndrome.
questions.modelAnswer: For Z1Z2: X2 anticommutes with the Z2 factor (X and Z anticommute on the same qubit) and commutes trivially with the Z1 factor (different qubit, so they act on disjoint qubits and simply commute). An operator product anticommutes with Z1Z2 overall if it anticommutes with an odd number of its tensor factors — here exactly one (Z2) — so X2 anticommutes with Z1Z2 as a whole, and measuring it flips to −1, i.e. syndrome bit 1. For Z2Z3: the same logic applies — X2 anticommutes with the Z2 factor and commutes with the Z3 factor (different qubit), again an odd count of anticommuting factors, so X2 anticommutes with Z2Z3 too, giving syndrome bit 1 as well. The resulting syndrome is (1,1), which matches the verified syndrome table directly: error on qubit 2 gives syndrome (Z1Z2,Z2Z3)=(1,1).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd work it one stabilizer at a time. X2 against Z1Z2: X and Z anticommute on the same qubit, so X2 flips the sign contributed by the Z2 part; it doesn't touch qubit 1 at all, so there's nothing to interact with there. One anticommuting factor is enough to flip the whole operator's sign, so Z1Z2 reads −1, i.e. a 1 bit. Same reasoning for Z2Z3 — X2 anticommutes with the Z2 factor there too, qubit 3 is untouched, so that's also a 1. Put together, that's syndrome (1,1), which is exactly what the table says happens for an error on qubit 2.
questions.example: Verified syndrome table (lesson 10): error on qubit 1 → (1,0); error on qubit 2 → (1,1); error on qubit 3 → (0,1); no error → (0,0).
commonMistakes: Forgetting that commuting with one factor and anticommuting with another still flips the whole product's sign if the anticommuting count is odd
Assuming X2 affects Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 identically without checking which qubit each operator actually touches
Mixing up which two stabilizers 'overlap' at qubit 2 (both do, which is exactly why qubit 2's error is detected by both)
keyPoints: X and Z anticommute on the same qubit; operators on different qubits commute
An operator anticommutes with a tensor-product stabilizer if it anticommutes with an odd number of factors
X2 anticommutes with both Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 because qubit 2 appears in both
This reproduces the verified syndrome (1,1) for an error on qubit 2

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly applies the anticommutation rule to Z1Z2
Correctly applies the anticommutation rule to Z2Z3
Arrives at the correct syndrome (1,1)
Clear step-by-step reasoning

questions.title: Why the 3-Qubit Bit-Flip Code Is Blind to Phase Errors
questions.prompt: The 3-qubit bit-flip code corrects any single X error perfectly but gives zero protection against a Z error. Explain the precise mechanical reason a Z error on any one qubit produces syndrome (0,0) — the same as no error at all — and why this means the logical state is corrupted undetected.
questions.modelAnswer: The stabilizers Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 are built entirely from Z operators. A Z operator always commutes with another Z operator on the same qubit (ZZ=ZZ), so a Z error on qubit 1, 2, or 3 commutes with both Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 regardless of which qubit it hits — there is no anticommutation event to trigger a syndrome flip. Both stabilizer measurements return +1, exactly as they would with no error present, so the syndrome reads (0,0) and the decoder concludes 'no correction needed.' Meanwhile the Z error has genuinely changed the relative phase of the encoded superposition α|000⟩+β|111⟩ (a Z on any one of the three qubits flips the sign of the |111⟩ component relative to |000⟩, since Z|1⟩=−|1⟩), so the logical state really has been corrupted — it's just corrupted in a way this particular code's stabilizers are structurally incapable of seeing, because they only ever check Z-basis agreement, which a Z error never disturbs.
questions.professionalAnswer: This code's whole detection mechanism is 'do these qubits agree in the Z basis,' and a Z error doesn't change any qubit's Z-basis value at all — it only flips a phase. Since the stabilizers are pure Z operators, and Z always commutes with Z on the same qubit, there's nothing for the stabilizer to detect; both measurements come back +1, syndrome (0,0), identical to the no-error case. But the logical state has changed — the relative sign between the |000⟩ and |111⟩ components has flipped — so you end up with a silently corrupted logical qubit and a syndrome table that insists everything is fine. That's exactly why a separate, complementary code built from X-type stabilizers is needed to catch phase errors.
questions.example: Starting from α|000⟩+β|111⟩, a Z error on qubit 1 produces α|000⟩−β|111⟩. Measuring Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 on this new state still returns +1 for both, because both |000⟩ and −|111⟩ remain +1 eigenstates of each Z-type stabilizer — the sign flip is invisible to a Z-basis parity check.
commonMistakes: Assuming any error must trigger some syndrome change
Confusing bit-flip and phase-flip errors' effects on measurement outcomes
Not recognizing that Z-type stabilizers are structurally blind to Z-type errors
keyPoints: Z commutes with Z on the same qubit, so Z errors never anticommute with Z-type stabilizers
A Z error changes relative phase, which pure Z-basis stabilizers cannot detect
Syndrome (0,0) after a real error is a silent corruption, not a confirmation of correctness
This motivates a complementary phase-flip code with X-type stabilizers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why Z errors commute with Z-type stabilizers
Explains what a Z error actually does to the logical superposition
Connects this to silent, undetected corruption
Clear, accurate explanation overall

questions.title: Stating the Threshold Theorem Precisely
questions.prompt: State the error threshold theorem precisely, including what happens on both sides of the threshold p_th. Then, using the course's illustrative scaling table (p_th=0.01, p=0.001, p_L ~ (p/p_th)^((d+1)/2)), explain why going from code distance d=7 to d=15 is described as 'a genuinely favorable trade' in terms of qubit cost versus error suppression.
questions.modelAnswer: The threshold theorem states that for a given code family, there exists a physical error rate p_th such that if the actual physical error rate p is below p_th, increasing the code distance d suppresses the logical error rate exponentially in d. If p is at or above p_th, increasing d does not help, and can actively make the logical error rate worse. This is a proven theoretical result for the surface code and related families — the actual numeric value of p_th for a given real device is a separate, empirical, hardware-specific question. Using the illustrative values, the table shows p_L falling from roughly 1.0×10⁻⁴ at d=7 to roughly 1.0×10⁻⁸ at d=15 — a 10,000x improvement in logical error suppression. The qubit cost (2d²−1) rises from 97 at d=7 to 449 at d=15, a 449/97 ≈ 4.6x increase in physical qubits. Paying roughly 4.6x more qubits to gain roughly 10,000x better error suppression is exactly the kind of trade the threshold theorem's exponential-vs-quadratic shape guarantees below threshold, which is why it's described as genuinely favorable rather than merely 'better.'
questions.professionalAnswer: The theorem says: below a certain physical error rate, scaling up the code distance buys you exponentially better logical error rates; above that rate, scaling up doesn't help and can actively hurt. It's proven math for the surface code family — what's not settled is what that threshold number actually is for any specific real chip, which is an engineering question, not a theory question. On the specific numbers: going from distance 7 to distance 15 costs about 4.6 times more physical qubits, but the illustrative scaling shows the logical error rate dropping by a factor of 10,000. That's an enormously lopsided trade in your favor — you're paying a linear-ish qubit cost increase for an exponential reliability gain, which is the entire economic argument for why fault-tolerant quantum computing is worth building toward at all, provided you're actually operating below threshold.
questions.example: Qubit cost: d=7 → 97 qubits, d=15 → 449 qubits (ratio ≈4.6x). Illustrative logical error rate: d=7 → ≈1.0×10⁻⁴, d=15 → ≈1.0×10⁻⁸ (ratio = 10,000x suppression).
commonMistakes: Stating the threshold theorem without mentioning the above-threshold regime explicitly gets worse, not just 'doesn't help'
Treating the illustrative p_th=0.01 as a real, universal hardware number rather than a teaching value
Confusing quadratic qubit-cost growth with the exponential logical-error suppression — they are different curves
keyPoints: Below p_th: increasing distance exponentially suppresses logical error rate
At or above p_th: increasing distance does not help and can make things worse
The theorem's existence is proven; the real numeric threshold is empirical and hardware-specific
d=7→15 costs ~4.6x more qubits for ~10,000x better illustrative error suppression

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States both the below- and at/above-threshold behavior correctly
Correctly distinguishes proven existence from empirical threshold value
Correctly computes/cites the qubit-cost vs. error-suppression trade
Clear, well-organized explanation

questions.title: Why the Steane Code's Self-Orthogonal Matrix Matters
questions.prompt: The Steane [[7,1,3]] code reuses the same Hamming(7,4) parity-check matrix H to generate both its 3 X-type and 3 Z-type stabilizer generators. Explain exactly why H being self-orthogonal (every pairwise row dot product, including a row with itself, is 0 mod 2) is the specific property that makes this reuse valid, in terms of what every stabilizer code requires of its generators.
questions.modelAnswer: Every stabilizer code requires all of its stabilizer generators to mutually commute, since only commuting operators can share simultaneous +1 eigenstates (the codespace). When you build an X-type stabilizer from row i of H and a Z-type stabilizer from row j of H, those two operators commute exactly when the rows overlap in an even number of qubit positions — because each overlapping position contributes one X-and-Z pair on the same qubit, which anticommutes, and an even number of individual anticommuting pairs multiplies out to an overall commuting relationship (each pair contributes a factor of −1, and an even count of −1 factors gives +1 overall). 'Dot product ≡ 0 mod 2' is precisely the statement that rows i and j overlap in an even number of positions. Because H is self-orthogonal, every pair of its rows — including a row with itself — satisfies this even-overlap condition, so every X-stabilizer commutes with every Z-stabilizer, including the matching pair built from the same row. That's what licenses reusing the same 3 rows for both types rather than needing 6 independent rows.
questions.professionalAnswer: The rule every stabilizer code has to satisfy is that all its generators commute with each other — that's what lets them all have simultaneous +1 eigenstates, which is the actual codespace. When you build one stabilizer out of Xs on certain qubits and another out of Zs on certain qubits, whether they commute comes down to how many qubits they share: an even number of shared qubits and they commute, odd and they anticommute. 'Self-orthogonal mod 2' is just a compact way of saying every pair of rows — including a row against itself — shares an even number of ones. So if H has that property, you can safely turn the same three rows into three X-stabilizers and three Z-stabilizers and know in advance they'll all commute with each other, without checking six independent rows for a brand new six-generator code.
questions.example: Row 1 of H is [0,0,0,1,1,1,1]. Its self-dot-product is 1+1+1+1=4≡0 mod 2, confirming it overlaps with itself in an even number of positions — this is exactly why the row-1-based X-stabilizer (X4X5X6X7) commutes with the row-1-based Z-stabilizer (Z4Z5Z6Z7).
commonMistakes: Thinking self-orthogonality is only about rows being distinct from each other, ignoring the 'row with itself' case
Not connecting 'dot product mod 2' to a literal count of shared qubit positions
Assuming any classical code's parity-check matrix could be reused this way without checking self-orthogonality
keyPoints: All stabilizer generators in a valid code must mutually commute
X-type and Z-type operators built from two rows commute iff those rows overlap in an even number of positions
Self-orthogonality guarantees this even-overlap property for every row pair, including a row with itself
This is what allows the same 3 rows of H to generate both the 3 X- and 3 Z-type stabilizers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the general commutation requirement for stabilizer generators
Explains the even-overlap commutation rule between X-type and Z-type operators
Connects self-orthogonality directly to licensing the reuse of the same rows
Clear, technically precise explanation

questions.title: Surface Code Qubit Count at Distance 19
questions.prompt: Using the verified surface-code formula total = 2d²−1 (data qubits = d², ancilla qubits = d²−1), compute the total physical qubit count for a distance-19 surface code. Then compare the absolute qubit increase from d=15 (449) to d=19 against the increase from d=3 (17) to d=7 (97), and explain why the increases are not the same size even though both represent a jump of the same relative step pattern (roughly doubling d).
questions.modelAnswer: Total at d=19: 2(19²)−1 = 2(361)−1 = 721 physical qubits. The increase from d=15 (449) to d=19 (721) is 721−449=272 qubits. The increase from d=3 (17) to d=7 (97) is 97−17=80 qubits. Even though both jumps roughly correspond to 'increase d by about 4-ish within a similar relative range,' the absolute qubit increase (272 vs 80) is more than three times larger at the higher distance range. This is the direct consequence of quadratic scaling: because total qubit count grows as d², the marginal qubit cost of each additional unit of distance itself grows as d increases — the derivative of d² with respect to d is 2d, which is larger at d=15-19 than at d=3-7. Quadratic growth means equal-sized steps in distance cost more and more additional qubits as the baseline distance gets larger, even though the growth is still far more favorable than the exponential growth of concatenated codes.
questions.professionalAnswer: Plugging into 2d²−1: distance 19 gives 2×361−1 = 721 qubits. Comparing jumps: 449 to 721 is a 272-qubit increase, while 17 to 97 was only an 80-qubit increase. Even though those are comparable 'jump sizes' in terms of how far d moved, the qubit cost of that jump is a lot bigger up at distance 15-19 than it was down at distance 3-7. That's just what a quadratic curve does — the slope gets steeper as you move right, so the same size step in d costs more total qubits the further out you already are. It's still way better than the concatenated code's exponential curve, but it's a reminder that 'quadratic' doesn't mean 'cheap at every scale,' just 'cheaper than exponential at every scale.'

Assuming quadratic growth means equal absolute increases for equal-sized steps in d
Confusing this with the exponential concatenation cost curve from the same chapter

The absolute qubit increase per step in d grows as d itself grows, because the curve is quadratic
d=15→19 costs more additional qubits (272) than d=3→7 did (80)
This is still far more favorable at scale than concatenation's exponential growth

questions.title: Distinguishing a Cited Literature Estimate From an Illustrative Worked Estimate
questions.prompt: The course cites Gidney & Ekerå's (2019) estimate of roughly 20 million physical qubits to factor RSA-2048 with Shor's algorithm, and separately walks through an illustrative calculation of 100 logical qubits × 449 physical qubits per logical qubit (at surface-code distance 15) = 44,900 physical qubits. Explain why these are fundamentally different kinds of numbers, and why it would be a mistake to treat the 44,900 figure as a simplified version of the Gidney & Ekerå result.
questions.modelAnswer: The Gidney & Ekerå figure is a literature citation: a specific, detailed engineering analysis of Shor's algorithm's actual circuit structure for factoring a 2048-bit RSA modulus, including real overheads like magic-state distillation, routing, and the specific gate sequence period-finding requires at that problem size. The 44,900 figure is this lesson's own illustrative arithmetic — a flat multiplication of (physical qubits per logical qubit) × (a round, hypothetical number of logical qubits, 100), used only to demonstrate the first-order method behind any resource estimate, not to model Shor's algorithm's real circuit at all. Treating 44,900 as a 'simplified Gidney & Ekerå' would be a mistake because the two numbers aren't answering the same question: one is a specific published result for a specific real algorithm at a specific real problem size (RSA-2048), and the other is a teaching example with an arbitrary hypothetical logical-qubit count that was never meant to reflect what Shor's algorithm at RSA-2048 scale would actually require. The flat multiplication also omits distillation overhead and other real costs that are central to why Gidney & Ekerå's number is as large as it is.
questions.professionalAnswer: These are two completely different categories of number, and keeping them separate matters. Gidney & Ekerå is a real, peer-reviewed estimate for a real, specific problem — factoring an actual RSA-2048 modulus with Shor's algorithm, including all the fault-tolerance overhead that comes with that specific circuit. The 44,900 number is just me demonstrating the mechanical idea — qubits per logical qubit times however many logical qubits you need — using a made-up round number, 100, that has no connection to what Shor's algorithm for RSA-2048 actually needs. If I called 44,900 'a simplified version' of the Gidney & Ekerå number, I'd be implying they're estimating the same thing at different levels of detail, when really one is a specific answer to a specific real question and the other is a generic illustration of the first-order math anyone would start from before adding in the real overheads.
questions.example: Gidney & Ekerå: ~20,000,000 qubits for RSA-2048, Shor's algorithm, ~8 hours. Illustrative: 100 hypothetical logical qubits × 449 qubits/logical qubit (d=15) = 44,900 qubits, a generic multiplication not tied to RSA-2048 or Shor's algorithm's real circuit.
commonMistakes: Treating the illustrative 44,900 figure as a rough version of the real RSA-2048 estimate
Not noticing the illustrative example uses a round, hypothetical logical-qubit count unconnected to any real algorithm
Assuming a flat multiplication captures the same overheads (distillation, routing) a real literature estimate accounts for
keyPoints: Gidney & Ekerå is a cited, published estimate for a specific real algorithm and problem size
The 44,900 figure is an illustrative, round-number teaching example of the underlying method
The two numbers are not approximations of the same quantity
A flat multiplication omits real overheads (distillation, routing) central to the literature estimate

questions.title: Deriving Shor's Algorithm Factors From a Period
questions.prompt: Walk through the algebraic proof behind Shor's algorithm: given that a is coprime to N and r is the multiplicative order of a mod N (the smallest r with a^r ≡ 1 mod N), explain step by step why an even r with a^(r/2) not ≡ -1 (mod N) guarantees that gcd(a^(r/2)-1, N) and gcd(a^(r/2)+1, N) are both nontrivial factors of N. Then verify this using N=15, a=7.
questions.modelAnswer: Start from a^r ≡ 1 (mod N), which rearranges to a^r − 1 ≡ 0 (mod N). When r is even, a^r−1 factors as a difference of squares: (a^(r/2)−1)(a^(r/2)+1). So N divides this product. Because r is the smallest exponent giving 1, a^(r/2) cannot itself be ≡ 1 (mod N) (that would make r/2 a smaller valid order, contradicting minimality), and by the added condition a^(r/2) is also not ≡ −1 (mod N). So neither factor (a^(r/2)−1) nor (a^(r/2)+1) is individually ≡ 0 (mod N) — yet N divides their product. The only way a number can divide a product without dividing either factor outright is if it shares a nontrivial piece of its own factorization with each factor separately — exactly what gcd(a^(r/2)−1, N) and gcd(a^(r/2)+1, N) extract, guaranteeing both are genuine, nontrivial divisors of N. Verification with N=15, a=7: powers of 7 mod 15 are 7,4,13,1, so r=4 (even). a^(r/2)=7²mod15=49mod15=4. Check 4 ≠ 14 (which is −1 mod 15), so the condition holds. gcd(4−1,15)=gcd(3,15)=3. gcd(4+1,15)=gcd(5,15)=5. Both are nontrivial, and 3×5=15, confirming the factorization.
questions.professionalAnswer: The whole proof rides on one piece of algebra: a^r−1 factors into (a^(r/2)−1)(a^(r/2)+1) whenever r is even, and we know N divides the left side because a^r≡1 mod N by definition of the order. If neither of those two factors is itself a multiple of N — which the order's minimality and the extra 'not ≡ −1' condition both guarantee — then N has to be splitting its factors across the two pieces, and gcd is exactly the tool that pulls out which piece goes where. Running the actual numbers for N=15, a=7: the order comes out to 4, which is even, good. 7 squared mod 15 is 4, and 4 isn't 14, so we're clear to proceed. gcd(3,15)=3 and gcd(5,15)=5 — both real factors, and sure enough 3 times 5 is 15.
commonMistakes: Forgetting why a^(r/2) cannot equal 1 mod N (minimality of the order)
Not explaining why the extra condition a^(r/2) ≢ -1 is needed alongside evenness
Skipping the logical step connecting 'N divides a product without dividing either factor' to gcd extracting nontrivial divisors
keyPoints: a^r−1 = (a^(r/2)−1)(a^(r/2)+1) when r is even (difference of squares)
Minimality of the order rules out a^(r/2) ≡ 1; the extra condition rules out a^(r/2) ≡ −1
N dividing a product without dividing either factor implies gcd extracts nontrivial divisors
N=15, a=7 gives r=4, a²mod15=4, factors 3 and 5

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states and uses the difference-of-squares factorization
Correctly explains why both the evenness and the ≠−1 condition are needed
Correctly reasons why gcd extracts nontrivial factors
Correctly works the N=15, a=7 verification

questions.title: Algorithm Correctness vs. Hardware Readiness for Shor's Algorithm
questions.prompt: Shor's algorithm has been physically demonstrated factoring small numbers like 15 and 21 on real quantum hardware, and the Gidney & Ekerå (2019) estimate for factoring RSA-2048 is roughly 20 million noisy physical qubits running for about 8 hours. Explain precisely why these two facts together do not imply RSA-2048 is close to being broken, and identify specifically whether the blocking factor is the algorithm or the hardware.
questions.modelAnswer: The demonstrations on N=15 and N=21 confirm that Shor's algorithm's mathematics and quantum circuit are correct and work exactly as proven — that is settled, not in question. But correctness at toy scale says nothing about resource requirements at cryptographic scale, because the resource requirements do not stay small as N grows — they scale with the size of N in a way that the Gidney & Ekerå analysis quantifies specifically for RSA-2048: roughly 20 million physical qubits. Real quantum hardware as of the mid-2020s has qubit counts in the tens to low thousands, several orders of magnitude short of that figure, and those physical qubits are themselves noisy, requiring substantial error-correction overhead (commonly hundreds to thousands of physical qubits per reliable logical qubit) just to run the deep, precise circuit Shor's algorithm needs at that scale without the computation falling apart to noise. Both gaps — raw qubit count and per-qubit reliability — compound rather than offset each other. The blocking factor is squarely engineering (building enough sufficiently reliable physical qubits), not mathematics (the algorithm's correctness and polynomial-time behavior were already proven and already demonstrated at small scale).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate the two claims clearly. 'The algorithm works' is proven and even demonstrated on real hardware for small numbers — that part isn't in dispute. 'RSA-2048 is breakable soon' doesn't follow from that, because the resource cost of running Shor's algorithm doesn't stay flat as the number you're factoring gets bigger — it scales up dramatically, and Gidney & Ekerå's detailed analysis puts RSA-2048 specifically at around 20 million physical qubits. Today's hardware is nowhere near that — we're talking orders of magnitude short, on top of the fact that today's qubits are noisy and need heavy error-correction overhead just to run reliably at all. So the honest framing is: the math was never the obstacle, it's been correct and demonstrated for over two decades. The obstacle is purely building enough reliable hardware, which is a long engineering road, not a missing insight.
questions.example: Toy demonstration: factoring N=15 or N=21 on real hardware, a handful of qubits. Cryptographic scale: Gidney & Ekerå's ~20 million qubits, ~8 hours, for RSA-2048 — many orders of magnitude beyond current hardware's tens-to-low-thousands of qubits.

Not distinguishing 'proven correct' from 'currently runnable at the needed scale'
Overlooking that noisy physical qubits need substantial error-correction overhead beyond raw qubit count

Gidney & Ekerå estimate ~20 million physical qubits for RSA-2048
Current hardware is orders of magnitude short on both raw qubit count and per-qubit reliability
The blocker is engineering (hardware scale and noise), not the algorithm's mathematics

questions.title: Why Lattice-Based Cryptography Resists Shor's Algorithm
questions.prompt: Explain structurally why Learning With Errors (LWE)-based schemes like ML-KEM are believed to resist Shor's algorithm, when RSA and discrete-log-based schemes do not. Be specific about what Shor's algorithm actually exploits and why that structure is absent from LWE.
questions.modelAnswer: Shor's algorithm's quantum speedup comes specifically from exploiting periodic structure: factoring is reduced to period-finding (finding the order r of a mod N), and the quantum Fourier transform efficiently extracts that hidden period. Discrete logarithm problems have an analogous periodic structure that a closely related quantum algorithm (also built on QFT-based period/phase estimation) exploits the same way. The Learning With Errors problem is structurally different: it asks you to recover a hidden vector from a system of linear equations that has had small, deliberate random noise added to each equation. Without the noise, this would be ordinary linear algebra, trivially solvable classically or quantumly. With the noise, there is no known periodic or algebraic structure analogous to modular exponentiation's order that a quantum Fourier transform could latch onto to extract the hidden vector efficiently. Because Shor's entire advantage is tied to exploiting that specific kind of periodicity, and LWE's hardness comes from noise obscuring linear structure rather than from any periodic structure, no known quantum algorithm — Shor's or otherwise — currently breaks LWE-based schemes efficiently. This is a belief based on the absence of a known attack, not a mathematical impossibility proof, consistent with how all cryptographic hardness assumptions are treated.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key is understanding what Shor's algorithm is actually built to find — a hidden period in a sequence, which the quantum Fourier transform is exceptionally good at extracting. RSA and discrete-log problems happen to have exactly that kind of periodic structure buried in them, which is why Shor's algorithm works on them. LWE just doesn't have that shape. It's a linear-algebra problem deliberately corrupted with small random noise, and there's no known period for a quantum Fourier transform to find — the noise itself is what makes the problem hard, not a hidden cycle. So it's not that LWE is immune to quantum computers in some absolute sense; it's that the specific tool Shor's algorithm uses doesn't have anything to grab onto here. And like any cryptographic hardness claim, it's 'no one's found an attack yet,' not a proof that none exists.
questions.example: RSA: factoring reduces to finding the period of a^k mod N — directly attackable by Shor's QFT-based period-finding. LWE: recovering a secret vector s from (A, As+e mod q) with small error e — no known periodic structure for a QFT-based approach to exploit.

Assuming any lattice problem is automatically quantum-resistant without the noise/structure distinction

questions.title: Why Grover's Optimal Iteration Count Cannot Be Exceeded Safely
questions.prompt: For N=8 with one marked item, the verified Grover trajectory shows P(marked) rising to 0.9453 at iteration 2, then falling to 0.3301 at iteration 3 and 0.0122 at iteration 4 — worse than the 0.1250 baseline of zero iterations. Explain the structural reason behind this non-monotonic behavior, and why it means Grover's algorithm cannot be run with 'extra iterations for safety' the way many classical algorithms can.
questions.modelAnswer: Each Grover iteration applies a fixed rotation of angle 2α (where sin α = 1/√N) to the state vector in the 2D subspace spanned by the marked and unmarked amplitudes. Because this rotation angle is constant per iteration rather than shrinking, repeated iterations don't converge toward the marked state and settle there — they keep rotating past it, continuing around the same geometric cycle. There is exactly one iteration count, t* = ⌊π/(4α)⌋ ≈ ⌊(π/4)√N⌋, where the state vector is closest to the marked state; iterations before that undershoot, and iterations after that overshoot, rotating back toward and eventually past the unmarked region, which is exactly what happens between iteration 2 (the peak) and iterations 3-4 in the N=8 trajectory. This is fundamentally different from algorithms like gradient descent that approach a fixed point and stay near it — Grover's probability trajectory is periodic, not convergent, so 'a few more iterations to be safe' can move you past the peak and back down toward, or even below, the original baseline probability, exactly as the N=8 data shows at iteration 4.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key insight is that each Grover step is a fixed-angle rotation, not a step that gets smaller as you approach the answer the way, say, gradient descent does. Since the rotation angle never shrinks, the state just keeps spinning around the same cycle forever — there's one specific point where it's closest to the marked outcome, and if you keep going past that point, you're rotating away from it again, not converging toward it. That's exactly what the N=8 numbers show: peak probability at iteration 2, then it drops, and by iteration 4 you're actually worse off than if you'd never run the algorithm at all. So you can't treat 'a couple extra iterations' as a harmless safety margin the way you might with most algorithms — here it can actively destroy your result, which is why you have to compute t* in advance and stop exactly there.
questions.example: N=8 verified trajectory: iteration 0 → P=0.1250 (baseline); iteration 1 → 0.7812; iteration 2 → 0.9453 (peak, matches t*=⌊(π/4)√8⌋=2); iteration 3 → 0.3301; iteration 4 → 0.0122 (worse than baseline).
commonMistakes: Assuming more Grover iterations are always at least harmless, as with most iterative algorithms
Not recognizing the rotation angle per iteration is fixed rather than shrinking
Describing the trajectory as monotonically improving rather than periodic

The probability trajectory is periodic, with exactly one optimal iteration count t*
Overshooting t* rotates the state back toward and past the unmarked region
Extra iterations can make results worse than doing nothing, unlike most iterative algorithms

questions.title: Deriving the Parameter-Shift Rule's Exact Gradient
questions.prompt: For a cost function g(θ) = sin(θ), use the parameter-shift rule df/dθ = [f(θ+π/2) − f(θ−π/2)]/2 to compute the gradient at θ = π/4. Show both shifted evaluations, the resulting gradient, and confirm it matches the calculus derivative g'(θ) = cos(θ) at that point. Then explain why the shift is exactly π/2 rather than an arbitrarily small number.
questions.modelAnswer: At θ=π/4: g(θ+π/2) = sin(π/4+π/2) = sin(3π/4) ≈ 0.7071. g(θ−π/2) = sin(π/4−π/2) = sin(−π/4) ≈ −0.7071. Applying the formula: df/dθ ≈ (0.7071 − (−0.7071))/2 = 1.4142/2 = 0.7071. The calculus derivative is g'(θ)=cos(θ), and cos(π/4) ≈ 0.7071 — the two methods agree exactly. The shift is exactly π/2, not an arbitrarily small number, because the parameter-shift rule is not a finite-difference approximation at all; it is an exact identity that holds specifically because the gate is generated by a Pauli operator with eigenvalues ±1 (so the generator in the exponent e^(-iθP/2) has eigenvalues ±1/2). That specific eigenvalue structure is what makes π/2 the exact value at which the formula reproduces the true derivative with zero approximation error, in contrast to classical finite differences, where accuracy depends on taking the shift ε to the limit ε→0 and smaller ε actually amplifies measurement noise on real hardware rather than improving accuracy.
questions.professionalAnswer: Plugging in: sin(3π/4) is about 0.7071, and sin(−π/4) is about −0.7071. Subtract and halve: (0.7071−(−0.7071))/2 = 0.7071. Compare that to the actual calculus answer, cos(π/4), which is also about 0.7071 — they match exactly. The reason the shift is fixed at π/2 rather than something you'd shrink for better accuracy, like a classical finite difference, is that this formula isn't an approximation in the first place — it's exact, and it's exact specifically because of the eigenvalue structure of the Pauli generator behind the gate. There's no accuracy to gain by using a smaller shift; in fact a smaller shift would just be the wrong formula and would expose you to more measurement noise for no benefit.

Treating π/2 as a tunable precision parameter like a classical finite-difference step size
Not connecting the exactness of the rule to the Pauli generator's ±1 eigenvalue structure
keyPoints: Parameter-shift gradient ≈0.7071, matching cos(π/4) exactly
π/2 is an exact value determined by the Pauli generator's eigenvalues, not a tunable precision knob
This is fundamentally different from classical finite-difference approximation

questions.title: Barren Plateaus as a Proven Result, Not a Concern
questions.prompt: Explain what McClean et al. (2018, Nature Communications) actually proved about barren plateaus, what specifically shrinks exponentially and with respect to what variable, and why this is described in the course as 'one of the best-established facts in the entire variational quantum computing literature' rather than a speculative concern.
questions.modelAnswer: McClean, Boixo, Smelyanskiy, Babbush, and Neven proved that for a broad class of randomly-initialized, sufficiently expressive variational circuits, the variance of the cost function's gradient — with respect to essentially every parameter in the circuit — shrinks exponentially as the number of qubits increases. This is a rigorous mathematical result about the structure of these circuits' parameter landscapes, not an empirical observation that might or might not generalize; it has been confirmed and extended by many follow-up papers (e.g., on the role of global vs. local cost functions, and on noise-induced variants). The statement is described as one of the best-established facts in the field precisely because it is a proven theorem about a well-defined class of circuits, in sharp contrast to the much less certain 'practical quantum advantage' claims that pervade popular and even some academic discourse around QML. Practically, this means that for a sufficiently wide, sufficiently expressive, randomly-initialized circuit, the parameter-shift rule still computes a mathematically correct gradient, but that gradient becomes so close to zero, and so easily swamped by finite-shot sampling noise, that gradient descent effectively stalls — not because of a bad local minimum in the classical sense, but because the landscape is almost perfectly flat almost everywhere.
questions.professionalAnswer: The 2018 Nature Communications paper is a genuine proof, not a hunch — it shows that for a wide class of variational circuits, started from random parameters and expressive enough to reach a large chunk of the full state space, the gradient's variance collapses exponentially as you add more qubits. That's a mathematical statement about the shape of the optimization landscape, confirmed since by plenty of follow-up work, which is exactly why this gets treated as settled science rather than a worry someone raised once. In practice it means: yes, you can still compute a gradient with the parameter-shift rule, but as the circuit scales up, that gradient becomes so tiny it's indistinguishable from the statistical noise in your measurements, and your optimizer just stops making progress — not because it's trapped in a bad spot, but because almost the entire landscape around it is essentially flat.
questions.example: A 6-qubit randomly-initialized, expressive variational circuit trains reasonably; naively scaling the same architecture to 60 qubits with the same random initialization runs directly into this proven exponential gradient-variance collapse, not a hypothetical risk.

Confusing gradient variance shrinking with the optimizer being stuck in a bad local minimum
Not specifying that the exponential shrinkage is specifically in the number of qubits

questions.title: The Variational Principle as VQE's Mathematical Guarantee
questions.prompt: State the variational principle precisely and explain why it guarantees that a classical optimizer minimizing ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ can never overshoot below the true ground-state energy. Using the worked 1-qubit example H = Z + 0.5X (true ground energy E_0 = −1.118034), explain why a reported trial energy of −1.2 for this specific Hamiltonian would be an immediate red flag.
questions.modelAnswer: The variational principle states that for any normalized trial state |ψ⟩, the expectation value ⟨ψ|H|ψ⟩ is always greater than or equal to the true ground-state energy E_0, with equality holding only when |ψ⟩ is exactly the ground state. This guarantees that searching for the trial state minimizing ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ can only ever approach E_0 from above — every candidate energy encountered during the search is a valid upper bound on the true answer, never below it, and the search converges to the exact answer only at the true minimizer. For H = Z + 0.5X, direct diagonalization gives eigenvalues ±√(1²+0.5²) = ±√1.25 = ±1.118034, so E_0 = −1.118034 is the smallest possible eigenvalue — mathematically, no valid quantum state of this system can have a lower expectation value than this, because E_0 is by definition the minimum of the spectrum. A reported trial energy of −1.2 is below E_0, which directly violates the variational principle; since the principle is a mathematical guarantee about any valid normalized state, this reported value cannot represent a correctly computed expectation value of a real quantum state against this Hamiltonian — it signals a bug (e.g., an incorrectly normalized state, a sign error in the Hamiltonian terms, or a measurement/implementation error), not a surprising new physical result.
questions.professionalAnswer: The variational principle is the guarantee that makes VQE work at all: for any valid trial state, the energy you measure is always at least as large as the true ground energy, and only equals it exactly at the true ground state. That means every number your optimizer sees during the search is a legitimate upper bound — you're always approaching the true answer from above, never below. For this specific Hamiltonian, diagonalizing it directly gives a true minimum energy of about −1.118034. If someone reports a trial energy of −1.2, that's below the provable floor — and because the variational principle isn't a rule of thumb, it's a mathematical fact about any normalized state, there's no legitimate way to get a number below E_0. That tells me immediately to go look for a bug — a state that isn't properly normalized, a mis-signed term in the Hamiltonian, or an error somewhere in how the expectation value was computed — rather than treating it as some kind of exotic quantum result.
questions.example: H = Z + 0.5X; eigenvalues = ±√(1+0.25) = ±1.118034; E_0 = −1.118034. The energy-vs-θ table in the worked example (1.0 at θ=0, 0.5 at θ=π/2, −1.0 at θ=π, −1.118034 at the optimum) never dips below −1.118034, consistent with the principle.

Treating a reported energy below E_0 as a surprising physical finding rather than a bug signal
Not connecting the principle to why VQE's search is guaranteed to approach from above

This guarantees VQE's search approaches E_0 from above, never overshoots below
E_0 = −1.118034 for H = Z + 0.5X, verified by direct diagonalization
A reported energy below E_0 is a mathematical impossibility signaling a bug, not a new result

questions.title: The T1/T2 Relationship and Its Physical Ceiling
questions.prompt: Using the relationship 1/T2 = 1/(2·T1) + 1/Tφ, explain why T2 can never exceed 2×T1, and determine whether a qubit reporting T1 = 150 microseconds and measured T2 = 90 microseconds is physically plausible. If it is plausible, estimate roughly what this implies about Tφ relative to T1.
questions.modelAnswer: Because 1/Tφ is always zero or positive (a time constant can't be negative, and the inverse of a very large or infinite Tφ approaches zero), the relationship 1/T2 = 1/(2T1) + 1/Tφ means 1/T2 is always at least 1/(2T1), which rearranges to T2 ≤ 2T1 always, with equality only in the ideal limit where pure dephasing is negligible (Tφ→∞). For T1=150μs, the ceiling is 2×150=300μs, and the measured T2=90μs is comfortably below that ceiling, so this result is physically plausible. To estimate Tφ: 1/T2 = 1/(2×150) + 1/Tφ → 1/90 = 1/300 + 1/Tφ → 1/Tφ = 1/90 − 1/300 ≈ 0.01111 − 0.00333 ≈ 0.00778, giving Tφ ≈ 128.6 microseconds — roughly comparable to T1 itself (around 0.86×T1), indicating that pure dephasing is contributing a meaningful, non-negligible fraction of the total decoherence rather than being negligible (which would push T2 close to the 300μs ceiling) or dominating overwhelmingly (which would push T2 much lower).
questions.professionalAnswer: The ceiling comes straight from the formula: since 1/Tφ can never be negative, 1/T2 is always at least 1/(2T1), which means T2 can never be more than twice T1. With T1 at 150 microseconds, that ceiling is 300 microseconds, and a measured T2 of 90 is well under that, so nothing's physically wrong here. Working backward to estimate Tφ: plug in the numbers, 1/90 minus 1/300, and that gives a Tφ of roughly 129 microseconds — which is in the same ballpark as T1 itself, not way bigger and not way smaller. That tells you pure dephasing is a real, meaningful contributor to this qubit's total decoherence, not something you could ignore, but it's also not so severe that it's crushing T2 down near zero.

Forgetting that 1/Tφ must be non-negative, which is the entire reason for the 2×T1 ceiling
Skipping the back-calculation of Tφ and only checking the ceiling without quantifying it

This indicates pure dephasing is a meaningful, non-negligible contributor to total decoherence

Include the oracle, the diffuser, and the measurement, and explain what probability distribution you expect when you run it on a simulator.

qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
# TODO: build the oracle and diffuser for a single Grover iteration
qc.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
questions.modelAnswer: The complete circuit is: qc.h([0,1]) for uniform superposition; qc.cz(0,1) as the oracle (phase-flips |11> only, leaving all probabilities at 0.25 since only a phase changed); then the diffuser qc.h([0,1]); qc.x([0,1]); qc.cz(0,1); qc.x([0,1]); qc.h([0,1]), which reflects every amplitude around the average, converting the phase flip into a measurable probability boost; finally qc.measure([0,1],[0,1]). For N=4, M=1, this specific case is exact: after one full iteration, the resulting state is exactly |11> with probability 1.0 and every other outcome at probability 0 — running this on a simulator should return the bitstring '11' on every single shot, with zero statistical spread, because the optimal iteration count formula (π/4)√(N/M) happens to evaluate to exactly 1 for N=4, M=1.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build it in three visible stages so it's easy to reason about: Hadamards for the uniform superposition, a controlled-Z as the oracle marking |11> with a phase flip, and then the standard five-gate diffuser (H, X, CZ, X, H on both qubits) to turn that phase flip into an amplitude boost. Then measure both qubits. For this exact case — 4 items, 1 marked, 1 iteration — the result isn't probabilistic in practice; it's deterministic. Every shot should come back '11'. That's actually a special, clean case; most real search spaces need more than one iteration and don't land on exactly probability 1.0, which is why I'd flag that this perfect result is the exception, not what to expect in general.

qc.cz(0, 1)

questions.title: Implementing Zero-Noise Extrapolation by Hand
questions.prompt: Given noisy expectation-value measurements E(1)=0.72 at normal noise and E(2)=0.64 at doubled (gate-folded) noise, write the linear zero-noise extrapolation calculation to estimate E(0), and explain what gate-folding operation you would apply to a gate G to actually produce the λ=2 measurement in the first place.
questions.code:
E1 = 0.72  # measured at lambda=1 (normal noise)
E2 = 0.64  # measured at lambda=2 (gate-folded, doubled noise)
# TODO: compute the linear zero-noise extrapolation E(0)
questions.modelAnswer: The linear extrapolation formula is E(0) = 2*E(1) - E(2). Plugging in: E(0) = 2*0.72 - 0.64 = 1.44 - 0.64 = 0.80. This recovers the ideal, zero-noise expectation value of 0.80 using only the two noisy measurements actually taken. To produce the λ=2 measurement in the first place via gate folding, you'd take a gate G in the circuit and replace it with G·G⁻¹·G — mathematically equivalent to G alone in the ideal, noiseless case (the inverse pair cancels exactly), but on real hardware each of the three gate executions carries its own real error, so the effective accumulated error roughly triples relative to a single G. Folding every gate in the circuit once this way is the standard way to reach λ=3 (triple noise); reaching λ=2 specifically typically means folding only a subset of gates, or using a partial-folding scheme, so that the effective noise scale lands at exactly double rather than triple.
questions.professionalAnswer: The arithmetic is just E(0) = 2*E(1) - E(2): double the λ=1 reading, subtract the λ=2 reading, and that's your estimate of what the circuit would have measured with zero noise — 2*0.72 - 0.64 = 0.80 here. To actually get that λ=2 data point on hardware, I'd use gate folding: take a gate G and run G followed by its own inverse followed by G again. In the ideal world that's exactly the same computation as just running G once, because G and G-inverse cancel — but on real noisy hardware, you've now executed three gates instead of one, so you've picked up roughly three times the error from that gate. A full fold of every gate typically triples the noise (λ=3); to land specifically at λ=2 you'd only partially fold, folding a chosen subset of gates rather than all of them.

# hand arithmetic: E0 = 2*0.72 - 0.64 = 0.80

questions.title: Writing a Statevector Test to Isolate a Circuit Logic Bug
questions.prompt: Write a Qiskit unit test using Statevector that checks a Bell-pair circuit produces exactly {'00': 0.5, '11': 0.5} with zero sampling noise. Then explain what it would mean, diagnostically, if this statevector test passes but a separate shot-based statistical test on the same circuit still fails.

from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

def test_bell_pair_statevector_is_exact():
    qc = build_bell_pair()
    # TODO: assert exact probabilities with no sampling noise
questions.modelAnswer:
def test_bell_pair_statevector_is_exact():
    qc = build_bell_pair()
    sv = Statevector.from_instruction(qc)
    probabilities = sv.probabilities_dict()
    assert set(probabilities.keys()) == {'00', '11'}
    assert abs(probabilities['00'] - 0.5) < 1e-9
    assert abs(probabilities['11'] - 0.5) < 1e-9

A statevector simulator returns exact amplitudes with zero sampling noise, so if this test passes, the circuit's underlying logic is confirmed correct — the bug, if the shot-based statistical test still fails, cannot be in the circuit's construction itself. It must be somewhere downstream: either the statistical test's tolerance was set too tight for the shot count actually used (producing false failures on genuinely correct code), or the failure is a real hardware/noisy-simulator effect rather than a logic bug, which should be confirmed by explicitly comparing the same circuit's noiseless result against its noisy-simulator or hardware result rather than assumed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The test itself is straightforward: build the Bell pair, pull its exact statevector, and check the probability dictionary has exactly '00' and '11' each at 0.5, with a tight numerical tolerance since there's no sampling noise to account for. If this passes, that's ground truth — the circuit's logic is correct, period, because a statevector simulator has zero sampling noise to hide behind. So if a shot-based test on the same circuit still fails after this passes, the bug can't be in how the circuit is built. I'd look next at whether the statistical test's tolerance was set correctly for the shot count in use, and only after ruling that out would I start suspecting a genuine hardware noise effect — and even then I'd confirm it by explicitly comparing noiseless vs. noisy results side by side rather than assuming.

questions.prompt: Given the course's QuantumBackend abstract base class (with abstract run(circuit, shots) -> dict and name() -> str methods), write a new concrete implementation for a hypothetical RigettiBackend that wraps a rigetti_client.submit(circuit, shots) call. Then explain why you should NOT add a get_calibration_data() method to the shared QuantumBackend interface just because Rigetti's hardware exposes one.

questions.prompt: Given 4 features (x1,x2,x3,x4) = (1.0, 0.4, 1.2, 0.8) in radians, write the qubit counts and the Qiskit-style construction logic for (a) angle encoding (one RY rotation per feature) and (b) amplitude encoding (normalize and load as amplitudes). Show the normalization arithmetic for the amplitude-encoding case.
questions.code:
features = [1.0, 0.4, 1.2, 0.8]
# TODO: angle encoding (4 qubits) and amplitude encoding (2 qubits) setup
questions.modelAnswer: Angle encoding needs 4 qubits, one RY(x_i) rotation gate per feature, applied in parallel with no entanglement required for the encoding step itself: for i in range(4): qc.ry(features[i], i). Qubit 1, for example, ends up in state [cos(0.5), sin(0.5)] ≈ [0.8776, 0.4794]. Amplitude encoding needs only 2 qubits, since 2²=4 amplitudes exactly fit 4 classical values. First normalize: norm = sqrt(1.0²+0.4²+1.2²+0.8²) = sqrt(1.0+0.16+1.44+0.64) = sqrt(3.24) = 1.8. Normalized vector ≈ (0.5556, 0.2222, 0.6667, 0.4444). In Qiskit: from qiskit.circuit.library import StatePreparation; qc.append(StatePreparation(normalized_vector), [0,1]). The qubit savings (4 vs 2) come at the cost of a deeper state-preparation circuit for amplitude encoding — potentially up to O(2^n) gates in the worst case for an arbitrary n-qubit state, versus angle encoding's constant-depth, one-gate-per-feature layer.
questions.professionalAnswer: For angle encoding, it's one RY gate per feature, so with 4 features you need 4 qubits and 4 independent, parallel rotation gates — no entanglement needed at all for the encoding itself. For amplitude encoding, the trick is that n qubits hold 2^n amplitudes, so 4 numbers fit into just 2 qubits. The catch is you first have to normalize your classical vector into a unit vector before you can load it as amplitudes — here that's dividing each value by sqrt(1.0²+0.4²+1.2²+0.8²), which comes out to 1.8, giving a normalized vector of roughly (0.556, 0.222, 0.667, 0.444). In Qiskit you'd hand that normalized vector to StatePreparation. The tradeoff is real: amplitude encoding needs fewer qubits but a potentially much deeper state-preparation circuit, so the 'savings' aren't free.

questions.title: Building the 3-Qubit Bit-Flip Code's Encoding and Syndrome Circuits
questions.prompt: Write a Qiskit circuit that (1) encodes an arbitrary single-qubit state into the 3-qubit bit-flip code using exactly two CNOT gates, and (2) adds the ancilla-based syndrome-extraction circuit for the Z1Z2 stabilizer (one ancilla, two CNOTs, one measurement). Explain what measurement outcome on the ancilla indicates an X error between qubits 1 and 2.
questions.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(4, 1)  # 3 data qubits + 1 ancilla, 1 classical bit for the syndrome
# TODO: encode qubit 0 into the 3-qubit bit-flip code, then extract the Z1Z2 syndrome
questions.modelAnswer:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(4, 1)
# Encoding: qubit 0 holds the data to protect; qubits 1,2 start at |0>
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.cx(0, 2)
# At this point the joint state is alpha|000> + beta|111> across qubits 0,1,2

# Syndrome extraction for Z1Z2 using qubit 3 as the ancilla
qc.cx(0, 3)
qc.cx(1, 3)
qc.measure(3, 0)

The two encoding CNOTs copy qubit 0's computational-basis value onto qubits 1 and 2, entangling all three into alpha|000>+beta|111> without cloning the quantum state. The syndrome circuit entangles the ancilla (qubit 3) to qubits 0 and 1 via two CNOTs: if qubits 0 and 1 agree (both effectively the same computational-basis value), the two CNOTs cancel on the ancilla and it measures 0 — no error. If qubits 0 and 1 disagree (an X error flipped one of them), the ancilla ends up flipped and measures 1, indicating an X error affecting the agreement between qubits 0 and 1.
questions.professionalAnswer: Encoding first: two CNOTs from the data qubit out to the two helper qubits spreads the single-qubit state into the entangled 3-qubit codeword, without ever cloning the actual quantum information — that's the standard move. For the syndrome, I add a fresh ancilla qubit, CNOT it from each of the two qubits I'm comparing, then measure just the ancilla. If those two data qubits still agree, the two CNOTs cancel out on the ancilla and it reads 0. If they disagree — meaning an X error flipped one of them — the ancilla picks up that disagreement and reads 1. That's the whole mechanism: a 0 or 1 classical bit telling you 'did these two qubits still agree,' without ever touching or revealing what the actual encoded superposition is.
questions.example: No error: ancilla CNOT'd to qubits 0,1 both in agreement → measures 0. X error on qubit 1 only: qubits 0,1 now disagree → ancilla measures 1, matching the verified syndrome table's (Z1Z2=1) entry.

Measuring a data qubit directly instead of the ancilla, which would collapse the protected superposition
Reversing which qubit is control vs. target in the encoding CNOTs
keyPoints: Encoding: two CNOTs (data->qubit1, data->qubit2) spread the state without cloning it
Syndrome: ancilla CNOT'd from both compared qubits, then measured alone
Ancilla measures 0 if the two data qubits agree, 1 if they disagree (indicating an X error)

questions.title: Debugging a Bell Pair With Roughly Equal 00/01/10/11 Counts
questions.prompt: A Bell-state statistical test fails, showing roughly equal counts of '00', '01', '10', and '11' instead of only '00'/'11'. Walk through the correct debugging order (construction check, then statevector, then tolerance, then noise) to diagnose this, and state what specific circuit bug most commonly produces exactly this symptom.
questions.modelAnswer: Following the correct order: first, re-run or inspect the construction test — check circuit.data directly. A near-uniform spread across all four outcomes (rather than, say, a slight skew that might suggest noise) is a strong signal of a logic bug rather than a hardware noise effect, since real decoherence noise on a well-constructed Bell pair typically shows a skew toward the correct outcomes with some leakage, not a flat distribution. The single most common construction bug producing exactly this symptom is a swapped control/target on the CX gate — e.g. CX(1,0) instead of the intended CX(0,1) — or, more subtly, applying the Hadamard to the wrong qubit before the CX, which can leave the two qubits essentially unentangled or entangled in a way that produces a flat rather than correlated distribution. Second, confirm with a noiseless statevector simulator: Statevector.from_instruction(qc) on the buggy circuit will show a state that is demonstrably not the Bell state (either unentangled, or entangled incorrectly), confirming this is a logic bug, not noise. Steps 3 (tolerance) and 4 (backend noise) don't need to be reached — the bug is found and confirmed at steps 1-2, which is the common case when the debugging order is followed rather than jumping straight to 'maybe it's the hardware.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start by blaming the hardware — a flat, roughly-equal spread across all four outcomes is actually a tell that points toward a logic bug rather than noise, since real noise on a correct Bell pair tends to skew toward the right answers with some leakage, not flatten out completely. My first move is to look at circuit.data and check the actual gate sequence — the single most common cause of exactly this symptom is a swapped control and target on the CX gate. Second, I'd confirm with a noiseless statevector simulation, which will show plainly that the circuit isn't producing an entangled Bell state at all if that's the bug. If both of those come back clean, only then would I move on to checking the statistical test's tolerance, and only after that would I seriously consider a real noise effect.

Treating a flat 4-way distribution as inherently a noise symptom rather than a logic-bug symptom
Not using a statevector simulator to get a noiseless ground-truth check before escalating

A flat 4-way distribution suggests a logic bug, not typical noise behavior

questions.title: Diagnosing a Faulty Syndrome Measurement in the Bit-Flip Code
questions.prompt: In the 3-qubit bit-flip code, the ancilla measuring Z1Z2 itself suffers a measurement error and reports the wrong bit, even though no actual X error occurred on the data qubits. Using the verified syndrome table (00=none, 10=qubit1, 11=qubit2, 01=qubit3), what incorrect correction would the decoder apply, and what would the resulting state actually be?
questions.modelAnswer: If no real error occurred, the true syndrome should be (0,0), meaning Z2Z3 correctly reports 0. But the faulty Z1Z2 ancilla reports 1 instead of the true 0, so the decoder observes syndrome (1,0). Consulting the table, (1,0) is the signature for 'error on qubit 1,' so the decoder incorrectly concludes qubit 1 needs an X correction applied, and applies it. Since no real error existed on the data before this, applying an unnecessary X-flip to qubit 1 actually introduces a genuine X error where none existed — the decoder's 'correction' is itself the source of the resulting corruption. The final state is the originally correct encoded state with qubit 1 now actually flipped, which is exactly a single X error on qubit 1 — recoverable in principle by a subsequent correct syndrome round, but a real error has now been introduced purely because the ancilla measurement itself was faulty, not because anything was wrong with the data to begin with.
questions.professionalAnswer: If the real syndrome should have been (0,0) — no error — but the Z1Z2 ancilla itself glitches and reports a 1, the decoder sees (1,0), which the table says means 'qubit 1 flipped.' So the decoder applies an X correction to qubit 1 that wasn't actually needed, and that correction itself becomes a real error — you've gone from a perfectly fine encoded state to one with an actual X error on qubit 1, purely because the ancilla measurement was wrong, not because anything happened to the data. This is exactly the scenario that motivates repeating syndrome extraction multiple rounds in real fault-tolerant protocols — a single faulty round can't be told apart from a real error just by looking at it once, so you need the consistency of multiple rounds to tell the difference.

Not recognizing that the 'incorrect correction' itself becomes the real error
Confusing which table entry corresponds to syndrome (1,0) versus (0,1) or (1,1)

(1,0) maps to 'correction: flip qubit 1' per the verified table
Applying this unnecessary correction introduces a real X error on qubit 1

questions.title: A Colleague Wants to Scale a Variational Classifier From 6 to 60 Qubits
questions.prompt: A colleague proposes scaling a variational classifier from 6 qubits to 60 qubits using the same randomly-initialized, generic hardware-efficient ansatz, expecting proportionally better accuracy. What specific, documented obstacle should you raise, and what would you ask them to show before believing training will succeed?
questions.modelAnswer: The specific, documented obstacle is the barren plateau phenomenon proven by McClean et al. (2018): for randomly-initialized, sufficiently expressive variational circuits, the gradient variance shrinks exponentially as qubit count increases. Going from 6 to 60 qubits is exactly the regime where this proven result applies most severely — a generic hardware-efficient ansatz with random initialization at 60 qubits is a textbook case for a barren plateau, where the parameter-shift rule still computes a technically correct gradient, but one so close to zero and so swamped by finite-shot sampling noise that gradient descent effectively stalls. Before believing training will succeed, I would ask the colleague to show: (1) what initialization strategy they're using (random initialization is specifically the regime the barren-plateau proof covers; smarter initialization like near-identity or layer-wise training can partially mitigate it), (2) whether the cost function is local (measured on a few qubits) or global (measured across all qubits), since global cost functions are documented to suffer worse plateaus, and (3) empirical evidence — an actual measured gradient-variance trend as qubit count increases for their specific ansatz, rather than an assumption that more qubits simply means proportionally better accuracy.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd bring up barren plateaus specifically, by name, and point to the fact that this isn't a maybe — McClean et al. proved in 2018 that for randomly-initialized, expressive circuits like this, gradient variance collapses exponentially as you add qubits. Jumping from 6 to 60 qubits with the same generic, randomly-initialized ansatz is close to a worst-case setup for exactly this problem. Before I'd believe this will train well, I'd want to see three things: what initialization they're using (random is the risky default), whether their cost function is measured locally or globally (global tends to be worse), and some actual empirical gradient-variance data at intermediate qubit counts, not just an assumption that scaling up qubits scales up accuracy proportionally — because the proven math says the opposite tends to happen without specific mitigations.
questions.example: A 6-qubit circuit training normally is not evidence that the same architecture will train at 60 qubits — the barren-plateau effect is specifically about how gradient variance behaves as qubit count scales, so small-scale success doesn't generalize without evidence.
commonMistakes: Treating 'add more qubits' as a purely resource/compute problem rather than a training-dynamics problem
Not naming the specific proven result (McClean et al. 2018) rather than a vague 'it might not scale well'
Failing to ask about initialization strategy or cost function locality, both documented mitigating factors
keyPoints: McClean et al. (2018) proved exponential gradient-variance shrinkage with qubit count for this exact setup
Random initialization and global cost functions specifically worsen the effect
6 to 60 qubits with a generic, randomly-initialized ansatz is a high-risk scenario for this obstacle
Ask for initialization strategy, cost-function locality, and empirical gradient-variance evidence

questions.title: A QAOA Run Performs Worse Than a Coin Flip
questions.prompt: A QAOA circuit on the single-edge Max-Cut problem is returning an expected cost of only ~0.519 (worse than a coin flip's worth of useful signal), while the same circuit structure achieves exactly 1.0 (optimal) at gamma=pi/2, beta=pi/8. The circuit's gates and oracle structure are confirmed correct. What is the most likely cause, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Since the circuit structure itself is confirmed correct and the only difference between the good and bad runs is the choice of angles (gamma, beta), the most likely cause is poor parameter selection — specifically, this matches the course's own verified comparison, where gamma=0.1, beta=0.1 gives expected cost ~0.519 while gamma=pi/2, beta=pi/8 gives exactly 1.0, using the identical circuit. QAOA is a variational algorithm: the gate structure is fixed, but the 2p numerical parameters are not, and they must be found via a classical optimization loop (or, for small/known cases, an exhaustive scan) rather than guessed or left at an arbitrary default like (0.1, 0.1). The fix is to run a classical optimizer (grid search for small p, or a gradient-based/gradient-free method like COBYLA or SPSA for larger p) over the (gamma, beta) landscape to find angles that actually maximize the expected cost, rather than assuming any fixed angle choice will work well across different problem instances or circuit depths.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since you've confirmed the gates themselves are right, this almost certainly isn't a construction bug — it's a parameter problem. QAOA's circuit shape is fixed, but gamma and beta are not something you can just guess at and expect good results; this looks exactly like the course's own comparison where (0.1, 0.1) gives you barely better than a coin flip while (pi/2, pi/8) gives you the true optimum, on the identical circuit. The fix is to actually run the classical optimization loop that QAOA is supposed to have — search over gamma and beta, either exhaustively for a small problem like this or with a real optimizer for anything bigger — rather than hardcoding a guessed pair of angles and expecting them to generalize.

questions.title: A VQE Loop Runs Three Hours With No Convergence and No Cost Alert
questions.prompt: A team's VQE loop has been running for three hours with no convergence and no cost alert triggered. Using the hybrid-architecture mistakes of (1) developing directly against real hardware, (3) no cost ceiling/circuit breaker, and (4) ignoring shot noise, write a short post-incident analysis explaining which of these mistakes most likely contributed and the specific classical-code fix for each.
questions.modelAnswer: Mistake 1 (developing directly against real hardware) likely contributed if this is still an early-development run: a half-finished, buggy version of the cost function or optimizer config run directly against real hardware for three hours burns real money and queue time on a loop that should have been debugged against a free classical simulator first. Fix: route all pre-production development and debugging through a classical simulator until the optimizer, cost function, and convergence logic are independently verified correct on toy problems, reserving real hardware for a small number of final validation runs. Mistake 3 (no cost ceiling or circuit breaker) is directly implicated by the fact that no cost alert triggered despite three hours of non-convergence — optimizers sometimes oscillate, plateau without tripping the tolerance check, or diverge due to a bug, and a loop with only a max-iteration cap but no cumulative-spend tracking can burn through budget silently. Fix: track cumulative spend inside the loop itself, not just after the fact in a billing dashboard, and halt with an alert if spend crosses a pre-set ceiling, independent of the iteration-count cap. Mistake 4 (ignoring shot noise) may be masking the real non-convergence: if the convergence check compares successive cost values without accounting for the ~1/sqrt(shots) standard error, small statistically-insignificant fluctuations can look like 'still improving' indefinitely, preventing the tolerance check from ever triggering. Fix: compare successive cost values against several standard errors, not a raw numerical tolerance that ignores shot noise.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through all three. First, if this loop hasn't been fully verified on a classical simulator yet, running a half-working version directly against real hardware for three hours is exactly mistake 1 — the fix going forward is: no real-hardware runs until the loop's logic is independently proven correct on a simulator. Second, the fact that nothing alerted after three hours is a direct symptom of mistake 3 — there's no circuit breaker tracking cumulative spend inside the loop itself, so it just kept going. The fix is adding that spend-tracking and a hard ceiling that halts the loop, not relying on a billing dashboard you only check after the fact. Third, if the convergence check is comparing raw cost values without accounting for shot noise, the loop might think it's still making progress when it's actually just bouncing around inside the ~1/sqrt(shots) measurement noise — the fix is requiring an improvement of several standard errors before considering the loop 'still converging,' not any raw numerical difference.

questions.title: SWAP Overhead Dominating a Circuit's Error Budget
questions.prompt: A circuit needing 40 native two-qubit gates requires 20 extra SWAP insertions once mapped onto a real device's connectivity graph. At a representative 0.5% per-gate error rate, roughly how much does total circuit error increase, and what does this imply is the largest single source of error in the computation? What are two concrete fixes?
questions.modelAnswer: Each SWAP costs roughly 3 CNOT-equivalents (built from 3 CNOTs on superconducting hardware), so 20 SWAPs add 60 CNOT-equivalents on top of the original 40 native gates, for 100 total two-qubit operations. At a representative 0.5% per-gate error rate, the 40-gate native circuit alone carries roughly an 18% chance of at least one error; adding the 60 extra SWAP-derived gates raises this to roughly 39% — more than double the original error risk, meaning routing overhead alone is responsible for more than half of the circuit's total error risk. This implies SWAP/routing overhead, not the algorithm's native gates, is the single largest source of error in this computation. Two concrete fixes: (1) use connectivity-aware qubit placement — map the circuit's logical qubits onto physical qubits whose native connectivity already matches the circuit's required interaction pattern as closely as possible, minimizing the number of SWAPs a router needs to insert in the first place; (2) invest in or tune the compiler's routing heuristic (e.g. Qiskit transpiler's routing pass with a higher optimization level, or trying multiple layout/routing seed combinations and keeping the lowest-SWAP-count result) rather than accepting the first valid mapping found, since heuristic routers can produce meaningfully different SWAP counts for the same circuit depending on their search strategy and starting point.
questions.professionalAnswer: Each SWAP is really three CNOTs under the hood, so 20 SWAPs is 60 extra two-qubit gates stacked on top of the original 40 — 100 total. At half a percent error per gate, the original 40-gate circuit alone already carries something like an 18% chance of at least one error somewhere; bring in those extra 60 SWAP-derived gates and that climbs to roughly 39%, more than double. So in this specific circuit, routing overhead isn't a minor tax — it's actually the single biggest source of error, bigger than the algorithm's own native gates. The two fixes I'd reach for: pick a better initial physical-qubit layout that already matches the circuit's natural connectivity needs, so the router has fewer SWAPs to insert in the first place, and don't settle for the first routing solution the compiler finds — try a higher optimization level or multiple routing attempts and keep whichever one actually inserts the fewest SWAPs.
