questions.title: Choosing Between Two Backends With the Same Median Error Rate
questions.prompt: Two backends from the same provider report similar median two-qubit gate error rates, but your circuit needs five qubits connected in a specific chain. What additional calibration-report data would you check before picking one backend over the other, and why would the median number alone not be enough?
questions.modelAnswer: The median error rate alone is insufficient because a chip's per-edge (two-qubit gate) error rates vary significantly across different connections — often spanning more than a factor of two between the best and worst edges on the same device. A device can have a very respectable median error rate while still lacking enough simultaneously good qubits and edges, in the specific 5-qubit chain connectivity pattern required, to actually run this circuit well. What to check instead: the specific per-edge error rates for the exact chain of 5 connections this circuit needs (not a device-wide average), the per-qubit T1/T2 for those specific 5 qubits (since the circuit's total runtime relative to those coherence times determines how much decoherence actually shows up in results), the readout error specifically on the qubits being measured at the end, and the last-calibrated timestamp for that specific region of the chip (since calibration data ages, and a report that's hours old may or may not still be trustworthy depending on that device's typical drift behavior). Only after comparing these specific, localized numbers for the actual 5-qubit chain on each candidate device can you make an informed choice — the device-wide median could easily hide one device having a uniquely good or uniquely bad 5-qubit chain available.
questions.professionalAnswer: The median is a device-wide summary, and it can easily hide exactly the information that matters for a specific circuit — if I need five qubits in a particular chain, what I actually care about is whether that specific chain of connections is good, not what the device looks like on average. So I'd pull the per-edge error rates for exactly those 5 connections on each backend, check T1 and T2 specifically for those 5 qubits against how long my circuit will actually run, check readout error on whichever qubits I'm measuring at the end, and check how recently that specific part of the chip was calibrated. A device could have a great median error rate overall while still not having five well-connected, low-error qubits sitting next to each other in the pattern I need — and that's exactly the gap the median number can't tell you about.
questions.example: Device A: median two-qubit error 0.4%, but the specific 5-qubit chain needed has one edge at 1.2% error. Device B: median two-qubit error 0.4%, with all 5 needed edges under 0.3%. The median alone would make these look identical; the specific edge data reveals Device B is the better choice for this circuit.

Not checking T1/T2 against the circuit's actual expected runtime
Ignoring the calibration timestamp's relevance to data freshness

questions.title: Diagnosing Retry-Storm Congestion From Fixed-Interval Retries
questions.prompt: A hybrid orchestration layer retries every failed quantum-job submission after exactly 1 second, with no variation. During a provider-side queue congestion event, failure rates spike across many concurrent clients and never recover. Explain the specific mechanism causing this, and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The mechanism is a retry storm: when many clients all experience a failure around the same time (because the root cause is shared, provider-side congestion), and every client retries on the exact same fixed 1-second interval, their retry attempts become synchronized — all hitting the already-struggling provider again at roughly the same moment, which adds more load rather than relieving it. This can create a self-sustaining cycle where the congestion that caused the first wave of failures is continuously reinforced by the synchronized retry wave itself, rather than naturally subsiding once the initial spike passes. The fix is exponential backoff with full jitter: each client's retry delay should grow with each successive attempt (roughly doubling) rather than staying fixed, and critically, each client should pick a randomized delay uniformly between 0 and the computed cap for that attempt rather than retrying at the exact computed value. The randomization is what desynchronizes simultaneous retriers — even if many clients fail at the exact same moment, their next retry attempts will be spread out across a range of times rather than landing together, which actually relieves pressure on the recovering provider instead of compounding it.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's happening is a retry storm — if a shared root cause (the provider's queue or rate limiter) knocks out a bunch of clients at roughly the same time, and they're all retrying after exactly the same fixed 1 second, they all hammer the provider again simultaneously. That just adds another spike of load right when the provider is already struggling, so the congestion never gets a chance to clear — the retries themselves are making it worse. The fix is exponential backoff with jitter: grow the delay with each attempt instead of keeping it fixed, and more importantly, randomize the actual delay within that growing window rather than retrying at the exact same computed time every client lands on. That randomization is the real fix here — it spreads retries out across time instead of letting them pile up together.
questions.example: 100 clients all fail at t=0 due to provider congestion. With fixed 1s retry: all 100 retry again at t=1, t=2, t=3... in lockstep, repeatedly re-spiking load. With full jitter exponential backoff: retries spread randomly across a growing window, e.g. some at t=0.3s, others at t=0.9s on attempt 1, desynchronizing the load.

Describing exponential backoff without jitter as a complete fix (it still synchronizes retriers without the randomization)
Not identifying that the shared root cause is what makes synchronized retries especially damaging

questions.title: Diagnosing a Calibration-Window Confound in an Unexpected Capstone Result
questions.prompt: A capstone hypothesis predicted that zero-noise-extrapolation's fidelity improvement would be smaller at 5 qubits than at 3 qubits. The actual data shows the opposite: the 5-qubit improvement (0.160) is slightly larger than the 3-qubit improvement (0.155). Construction and parameter checks both come back clean. What should you check next, and what would finding it mean for how you report the result?
questions.modelAnswer: With implementation bugs and parameter mismatches both ruled out, the next thing to check is whether the two conditions (3-qubit and 5-qubit runs) were actually executed under comparable device states — specifically, whether they were genuinely interleaved in time, or whether a queue delay or scheduled recalibration separated them onto different calibration windows. This matters because a device's real error characteristics can shift meaningfully between calibration windows, and if the 5-qubit jobs ran, say, six hours after the 3-qubit jobs, immediately following a recalibration, the comparison is confounded by device-state differences that have nothing to do with qubit count itself. Finding this would mean the most likely explanation isn't that the proposed mechanism (more gates, more accumulated noise shrinking mitigation's benefit as qubit count grows) is wrong — it's that the experimental design didn't actually hold the device state constant across the two conditions being compared, which is exactly the confound that interleaving runs within one calibration window exists to prevent. Reporting this honestly means stating that the direction-of-effect claim (mitigation helps at both counts) is still supported, but the relative-magnitude claim is not supported under these specific run conditions, and naming the calibration-window gap explicitly as the likely confound in the limitations section — rather than either hiding the contradiction or over-claiming that it disproves the underlying mechanism.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since the usual first suspects — implementation bugs, parameter mismatches — are already ruled out, I'd look at whether the two conditions were actually run under the same device conditions. Specifically: were the 3-qubit and 5-qubit jobs genuinely interleaved, or did one batch run hours later than the other, maybe right after the device got recalibrated? If that's what happened, the honest conclusion isn't 'the hypothesis about accumulated noise is wrong' — it's that the comparison itself wasn't a clean one, because the device wasn't in a comparable state across the two conditions. I'd report that plainly: the basic direction of the effect still holds, but the specific magnitude comparison isn't trustworthy given this gap, and I'd name the calibration-window issue explicitly in the limitations section rather than either burying the contradiction or claiming it disproves anything about the underlying mechanism.
questions.example: Run log shows: 3-qubit jobs ran at 2:00pm; 5-qubit jobs ran at 8:00pm, after a scheduled device recalibration at 6:00pm — the two conditions were never run under the same calibration window.
commonMistakes: Jumping to 'the hypothesis is falsified' without checking for a design/execution confound first
Quietly reframing the hypothesis after the fact to match the unexpected result (HARKing) instead of reporting the contradiction honestly
Not naming the specific confound explicitly in the limitations section
keyPoints: After ruling out bugs and parameter mismatches, check whether conditions ran under comparable device states
A calibration-window gap between the two conditions is a classic confound, not a disproven hypothesis
The direction-of-effect claim can remain supported while the relative-magnitude claim is not
Honest reporting names the confound explicitly rather than hiding or over-interpreting it

Correctly distinguishes a design/execution confound from a falsified hypothesis

questions.title: A Statistical Test Fails but the Statevector Simulator Shows a Perfect State
questions.prompt: A statistical test for a 2-qubit circuit expected to produce only '01' (never '00', '10', or '11') is failing on real hardware. The statevector simulator shows the exact state |01> with probability 1.0. What does this tell you about where the bug is, and which debugging step would you move to next?
questions.modelAnswer: A statevector simulator returning the exact state |01> with probability 1.0 definitively rules out a circuit construction or logic bug — the statevector simulator has zero sampling noise, so if the ideal circuit logic were wrong, this check would have failed. Since the logic is confirmed correct, the failing statistical test on real hardware is not a logic bug; it is either a test-tolerance mismatch (the statistical test's tolerance for an acceptable deviation might be too tight for the shot count actually used, causing it to flag normal sampling and/or hardware-noise variation as a failure) or a genuine backend/noise effect (real hardware naturally introduces decoherence, gate errors, and readout error, which can shift the measured distribution away from the ideal {'01': 1.0} even with perfectly correct circuit logic). The correct next step is to check the test's tolerance against the shot count used (step 3 in the debugging order), and only after confirming the tolerance is appropriately set should you conclude the discrepancy is a real hardware noise effect (step 4) — ideally confirmed explicitly by comparing the same circuit's noiseless-simulator result against its noisy-simulator or real-hardware result side by side, rather than assumed.
questions.professionalAnswer: Getting an exact, noiseless |01> at probability 1.0 from the statevector simulator tells me the circuit's logic is completely correct — there's no bug to find in the construction, full stop, because that simulator has no sampling noise to hide behind. So whatever's causing the real-hardware test to fail isn't in the circuit itself. The next place I'd look is the statistical test's tolerance — was it set tight enough that normal sampling variation or minor hardware noise would trip it even on a correct circuit? Only after I've confirmed the tolerance is reasonable for the shot count in use would I actually attribute the failure to real hardware noise, and even then I'd want to see that confirmed directly by comparing the noiseless and noisy results side by side rather than just assuming it.
questions.example: If the statistical test asserts P('01') > 0.98 with only 50 shots, normal binomial sampling variation alone could occasionally produce a measured proportion below 0.98 even on perfectly correct hardware and circuit logic — a tolerance/shot-count mismatch, not a bug.
commonMistakes: Concluding real hardware noise is automatically the cause without first checking the test's tolerance
Not recognizing that a passing noiseless statevector check fully rules out a circuit logic bug
Re-checking circuit construction again instead of moving forward to tolerance, since construction is already confirmed correct via the statevector result
keyPoints: A passing statevector check with zero sampling noise rules out a circuit construction/logic bug entirely
The next step is checking the statistical test's tolerance against the shot count used
Only after ruling out tolerance mismatch should a real hardware noise effect be concluded
Confirm any suspected noise effect by explicit side-by-side comparison, not assumption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly concludes the circuit logic is not the bug
Correctly identifies tolerance mismatch as the next thing to check
Correctly places real hardware noise as the last step to consider, and only with confirmation
Clear, well-organized explanation

questions.title: Spotting a Weak-Baseline Benchmark Claim
questions.prompt: A paper claims 'our QAOA implementation found a better Max-Cut solution than classical search in fewer iterations.' Using the course's four benchmark failure modes (weak baseline, query count without query cost, cherry-picked instance, excluded classical overhead) and its checklist, list the specific questions you would need answered before accepting this claim as fair and meaningful.
questions.modelAnswer: Four specific questions map directly to the four failure modes: (1) Weak baseline — what specific classical method is 'classical search' here? If it's an unoptimized greedy or random search rather than simulated annealing or a tuned commercial solver, the comparison may just be beating a strawman rather than the best classical method reasonably available. (2) Query cost vs. query count — 'fewer iterations' is a query-count claim; is each quantum query's wall-clock cost comparable to a classical iteration's, or is each QAOA circuit evaluation (including its own classical optimizer overhead) actually slower in practice, making the 'fewer iterations' framing misleading about real elapsed time? (3) Cherry-picked instance — what problem size and specific graph instance was tested? A result on a small, specially-structured graph doesn't imply anything about performance at realistic scale without separately testing that scale. (4) Excluded classical overhead — does the reported timing/iteration count for the QAOA side include the full pipeline (QUBO construction, Ising conversion, circuit construction, and the classical parameter optimizer's own iterations across potentially many circuit evaluations), or does it count only the 'quantum part,' leaving out real costs that a complete classical pipeline would need to be compared against on equal footing? A benchmark that answers all four of these transparently is rare and worth taking seriously; one that doesn't should not be accepted as a meaningful quantum-advantage claim.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask four specific things, one per failure mode the course covers. First, what exactly is 'classical search' here — is it the strongest classical method reasonably available, or something weak like unoptimized greedy search that makes any result look good by comparison? Second, 'fewer iterations' is a query-count claim, not a cost claim — were the iterations actually cheaper in wall-clock time too, or just fewer in number while each one took longer? Third, what size and which specific problem instance was tested — is this a cherry-picked small case, and has it been shown to hold at any realistic scale? Fourth, does the quantum side's timing include the full pipeline — QUBO setup, the classical optimizer loop driving the circuit evaluations — or does it only count the quantum circuit itself, leaving out costs a fair comparison needs on both sides? Until those four are answered, I wouldn't treat this as a meaningful quantum-advantage result either way.
questions.example: A result reporting 'QAOA beat classical search in iterations' on a 4-node graph, timed excluding the classical optimizer's own overhead, against an unoptimized greedy baseline, would fail all four checks simultaneously.
commonMistakes: Accepting 'fewer iterations' as proof of a real speedup without asking about per-iteration cost
Not asking what specific classical method 'classical search' actually refers to
Failing to ask whether the reported quantum-side cost includes the classical optimizer's own overhead
keyPoints: Ask what specific classical method was used as the baseline, and whether it is the strongest reasonably available
Ask whether per-iteration cost, not just iteration count, was reported and compared fairly
Ask what problem size/instance was tested and whether it generalizes to realistic scale
Ask whether the full pipeline, including classical optimizer overhead, was timed on both sides

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly raises the weak-baseline question
Correctly raises the query-count-vs-cost question
Correctly raises the cherry-picked-instance question
Correctly raises the excluded-overhead question

questions.title: An Implausible T1/T2 Calibration Reading
questions.prompt: A calibration report lists a qubit's T1 as 80 microseconds and T2 as 190 microseconds. Using the relationship 1/T2 = 1/(2*T1) + 1/T_phi, is this reading physically plausible? If not, what does it most likely indicate, and what would you do before trusting any run on this qubit?
questions.modelAnswer: The physical ceiling is T2 <= 2*T1. With T1=80 microseconds, the ceiling is 2x80=160 microseconds. A reported T2 of 190 microseconds exceeds that ceiling, which is not physically plausible under the standard relationship — since 1/T_phi must be zero or positive, T2 can never exceed 2*T1. This most likely indicates either a measurement/calibration error in how T1 or T2 was measured (e.g. a Ramsey or spin-echo experiment for T2, or a relaxation experiment for T1, that was run under different or inconsistent conditions, or affected by a separate error such as low-frequency drift during the measurement itself), a stale or mismatched calibration report (the two numbers may have been measured at different times, under different device states, and simply don't belong together), or a data-entry/reporting bug in the published report rather than a real physical measurement. Before trusting any run on this qubit, you should not proceed based on this report alone — check the last-calibrated timestamps for both the T1 and T2 entries specifically (they may not actually be from the same calibration pass), consider re-requesting or re-running the calibration if the platform allows it, and treat this device/qubit as suspect (closer to 'possibly degraded or misreported' than 'currently reliable') until a self-consistent pair of T1/T2 values is confirmed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The math sets a hard ceiling: T2 can never be more than twice T1, because the extra dephasing term in the formula can only add to the dephasing rate, never subtract from it. With T1 at 80 microseconds, that ceiling is 160, and a reported T2 of 190 is past it — so this isn't physically possible as stated. My first guess wouldn't be 'exotic new physics,' it would be that these two numbers weren't actually measured together — maybe they're from different calibration passes, or there was a glitch in one of the two individual measurement procedures, or it's just a reporting error in the published data. Before I'd run anything real on this qubit, I'd check whether the T1 and T2 timestamps actually match, try to get a fresh calibration if that's available, and treat this specific qubit as unreliable until I see a self-consistent pair of numbers.
questions.example: T1=80us -> ceiling 2*T1=160us. Reported T2=190us exceeds this ceiling, violating 1/T2 = 1/(2*T1) + 1/T_phi (which requires T2 <= 2*T1 always).
commonMistakes: Accepting the reported numbers at face value without checking the T2 <= 2*T1 constraint
Assuming an implausible reading means something exotic rather than a measurement/reporting error
Proceeding with a run on the qubit without first investigating the inconsistency
keyPoints: T2 <= 2*T1 always, since 1/T_phi cannot be negative
T1=80us gives a ceiling of 160us; a reported T2=190us violates this and is not plausible
Most likely explanation is a measurement, timing-mismatch, or reporting error, not real physics
Do not trust a run on this qubit until the inconsistency is resolved or a fresh, consistent calibration is obtained

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the 2*T1 ceiling and identifies the violation
Correctly concludes this is not physically plausible as reported
Proposes plausible causes (measurement/timing/reporting error)
Proposes a concrete next step before trusting the qubit

questions.title: A Hybrid Project Can't Switch Providers Without a Rewrite
questions.prompt: Your team's classical orchestration code calls AWS Braket's SDK directly throughout the codebase. A pricing change makes a different provider more cost-effective, but switching requires rewriting most of the orchestration layer. What specific architecture mistake caused this, and what is the concrete fix?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a direct instance of tight coupling between orchestration code and one provider's SDK — a documented hybrid-architecture mistake. Because the classical loop calls AWS Braket's SDK directly throughout the codebase rather than through an internal abstraction, every place that touches circuit submission, job status, or result retrieval is written in terms of Braket-specific calls, so switching providers means finding and rewriting all of those call sites rather than changing one small piece. The concrete fix is to define a thin internal interface — e.g. submit_circuit(), get_result(), estimate_cost() — that the classical loop calls exclusively, with provider-specific adapter classes (a BraketAdapter today, an IonQAdapter or RigettiAdapter tomorrow) implementing that interface behind the scenes. This is standard dependency inversion applied to this domain: the orchestration logic depends only on the interface, never on a specific provider's SDK types or calls, so adding or switching a provider becomes a matter of writing one new adapter class and changing a configuration value, not rewriting the orchestration layer itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is exactly the tight-coupling-to-one-SDK mistake — writing directly against Braket's API everywhere felt faster at the time, but now a pricing change means a provider switch has turned into a full rewrite of the orchestration code, which is the predictable cost of that shortcut. The fix is to introduce a thin internal interface — something like submit_circuit, get_result, estimate_cost — and have the orchestration logic only ever call that interface, never Braket directly. Then a Braket-specific adapter implements it today, and if we need to add or switch to another provider later, that's a new adapter class, not a rewrite of the whole orchestration layer. It's the same dependency-inversion pattern you'd use in any non-quantum backend system, just applied here.
questions.example: Before: orchestration code calls braket_client.create_quantum_task(...) directly in a dozen places. After: orchestration code calls backend.submit_circuit(...), where backend is a BraketAdapter today and could be an IonQAdapter tomorrow, with zero changes to the orchestration logic itself.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a problem requiring a quantum-specific fix rather than standard software engineering practice
Proposing a one-off migration script instead of a reusable abstraction layer that prevents the same problem next time
Not naming dependency inversion/the adapter pattern explicitly as the applicable fix
keyPoints: Tight coupling to one provider's SDK is a documented hybrid-architecture mistake
The fix is a thin internal interface (submit_circuit, get_result, estimate_cost)
Provider-specific adapters implement that interface behind the scenes
This is standard dependency inversion, not a quantum-specific fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies tight SDK coupling as the root cause
Proposes the correct fix (thin internal interface + provider adapters)
Correctly frames this as standard dependency inversion
Clear, practical explanation

questions.title: A Grover Search Got Worse After 'Adding a Safety Margin'
questions.prompt: A teammate ran a Grover search on an N=8, single-marked-item space at the formula-derived optimal 2 iterations, got 94.53% success, then re-ran it with 2 extra 'safety margin' iterations (4 total) expecting an even better or at least equally good result, but got only 1.22% success. Diagnose exactly what happened and explain why this is a quantum-specific risk that wouldn't occur with most classical iterative methods.
questions.modelAnswer: This is not a bug — it is the expected, mathematically predictable consequence of Grover's algorithm's periodic rotation structure. Each iteration rotates the state vector by a fixed angle 2*alpha toward the marked state; for N=8 with one marked item, the optimal iteration count is t* = floor((pi/4)*sqrt(8)) = 2, which is exactly where the verified trajectory peaks at 94.53%. Running 2 additional iterations doesn't add 'more of the same good effect' — it continues the same fixed-angle rotation past the peak, through iteration 3 (33.01%, already worse than iteration 1) and on to iteration 4, where the state has rotated almost all the way back around, landing at just 1.22% — worse than doing zero iterations at all (12.5% baseline). This is a quantum-specific risk because, unlike gradient descent or most classical iterative refinement methods, which approach a fixed point and tend to stay near it (so extra iterations are typically harmless or merely wasteful), Grover's state vector never converges and sits at the marked state — it keeps rotating through a periodic cycle indefinitely, so there is no 'safety margin' available by running extra iterations. The only correct approach is computing t* precisely in advance from the known or estimated search-space size and stopping exactly there.
questions.professionalAnswer: What happened is completely predictable, not a glitch: Grover rotates the state by a fixed angle every iteration, and for an 8-item space with one marked item, iteration 2 is exactly the peak of that rotation — 94.53% success. Running two more iterations doesn't add extra safety margin the way it would in, say, gradient descent, because the rotation doesn't stop or slow down once it reaches the best point; it just keeps going, swings past the target, and by iteration 4 has rotated almost all the way back around, landing at barely over 1%, which is actually worse than not running the algorithm at all. The reason this is quantum-specific is that most classical iterative methods converge to a fixed point and plateau there, so running extra iterations is usually harmless. Grover's probability trajectory is periodic, not convergent — there's exactly one right stopping point, computed in advance from the formula, and no amount of 'extra iterations to be safe' can substitute for getting that number right.
questions.example: N=8 verified trajectory: iteration 2 -> 94.53% (peak, = t*); iteration 3 -> 33.01%; iteration 4 -> 1.22% (worse than the 12.5% zero-iteration baseline).
commonMistakes: Treating this as a bug to fix in the circuit rather than an expected consequence of running past t*
Assuming 'more iterations' is always at least harmless, as with most classical iterative algorithms
Not computing or citing the exact optimal iteration count (t*=2 for N=8) to frame the explanation
keyPoints: Each Grover iteration is a fixed-angle rotation; t*=floor((pi/4)sqrt(N)) is the single optimal point
Running past t* doesn't add safety margin — it continues rotating past the marked state
iteration 4's 1.22% is worse than even the zero-iteration 12.5% baseline
This is quantum-specific because the trajectory is periodic, not convergent like most classical methods

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies this as expected periodic behavior, not a bug
Correctly explains the fixed-rotation-angle mechanism
Correctly contrasts this with convergent classical iterative methods
Clear, accurate overall diagnosis

questions.title: Designing a Backend Abstraction That Resists Capability Leakage
questions.prompt: You're designing the QuantumBackend interface for a new project that must support a local simulator, a noisy simulator, and two real hardware providers. A teammate wants to add get_queue_position() to the shared interface so 'all backends have it.' Design the correct architecture: what belongs in the shared interface, what doesn't, and where hardware-specific capabilities like queue position should live instead.
questions.modelAnswer: The shared QuantumBackend interface should contain only the contract every backend can meaningfully satisfy identically: run(circuit, shots) -> dict and name() -> str, matching the course's established pattern. get_queue_position() should NOT be added to this shared interface, because a local or noisy simulator has no real queue to report a position in — adding it there forces either a meaningless fake return value (e.g. always 0) for simulators, or an exception that algorithm code now has to special-case, both of which erode the guarantee that every backend implementing the interface behaves uniformly. This is capability leakage: a hardware-specific feature polluting a contract meant to be uniformly implementable. The correct architecture is a separate, optional interface — e.g. QueueableBackend with get_queue_position() — that only the real hardware backend classes implement, alongside the base QuantumBackend. Algorithm code written generically against QuantumBackend never touches queue position at all; code that specifically knows it's targeting real hardware can check isinstance(backend, QueueableBackend) (or use a hardware-specific subclass directly) and call get_queue_position() only in that branch. This keeps the common contract clean and uniformly satisfiable while still exposing the hardware-specific capability to the code that actually needs it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on adding it to the shared interface, for the same reason the course's backend-abstraction lesson flags this exact scenario: a simulator just doesn't have a queue, so there's nothing honest to return for get_queue_position() there. The shared interface should stay limited to what every backend can do the same way — run a circuit, report its name — and anything hardware-specific, like queue position, calibration data, or qubit-specific error rates, belongs in a separate, optional interface that only the real hardware backends implement. Generic algorithm code never needs to know that interface exists; code that's specifically working with real hardware, and knows it, can reach for it deliberately. That split keeps the main contract clean and genuinely uniform across every backend, instead of slowly accumulating hardware-only methods that half the implementations have to fake.
questions.example: class QuantumBackend(ABC): run(), name() — implemented identically by every backend. class QueueableBackend(ABC): get_queue_position() — implemented only by IBMHardwareBackend, RigettiBackend, etc., never by LocalSimulatorBackend.
commonMistakes: Adding hardware-only methods to the shared interface 'for convenience' and faking return values for simulators
Making every backend throw NotImplementedError for methods it can't meaningfully support, breaking uniform substitutability
Not proposing a concrete alternative location (a separate interface or subclass) for the hardware-specific capability
keyPoints: Shared interface should contain only universally, identically satisfiable methods (run, name)
get_queue_position() is capability leakage if added to the shared interface
A separate, optional interface (e.g. QueueableBackend) should hold hardware-specific capabilities
Generic algorithm code stays simple; hardware-aware code opts into the extra interface deliberately

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies get_queue_position() as capability leakage if added to the shared interface
Correctly designs a separate interface/subclass for hardware-specific capabilities
Explains how algorithm code interacts with each interface appropriately
Clear, well-organized architectural reasoning

questions.title: Choosing QAOA Circuit Depth Under a Noise-Depth Tradeoff
questions.prompt: You're deploying a QAOA solution for a real optimization problem on current NISQ hardware with representative gate fidelities of 99.0-99.9%. The depth-1 vs depth-2 comparison on the 4-cycle Max-Cut problem showed approximation ratio rising from ~0.75 (p=1) to ~0.9999 (p=2) on a noiseless simulator. Design your approach to choosing p for a real hardware deployment, explaining what additional information you need before committing to p=2 or higher.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture decision cannot be made from the noiseless simulation result alone, because that result only tells you the theoretical approximation-ratio ceiling at each depth — it says nothing about how much real hardware noise erodes that ceiling as depth (and therefore gate count) increases. The correct approach: (1) first establish the noiseless approximation ratio at each candidate depth (already done: 0.75 at p=1, 0.9999 at p=2) as the theoretical best case; (2) separately measure or estimate the actual gate count and circuit depth each p value requires on the target hardware, including any SWAP/routing overhead from that device's connectivity; (3) using the device's actual calibration data (per-gate fidelity, not just the generic 99.0-99.9% range), estimate the realistic probability that the deeper p=2 circuit survives execution without an error outweighing its theoretical approximation-ratio advantage — since each additional layer adds exactly 2 more parameters and more real quantum gates, each with nonzero error probability; (4) run both p=1 and p=2 empirically on the actual target device (or a noisy simulator calibrated to it) and compare the real measured approximation ratios, not just the noiseless ones, before committing. The decision is not 'is more depth theoretically better' (it provably is, as p approaches infinity) but 'does this specific device's noise profile let the deeper circuit's theoretical advantage survive in practice' — which can only be answered with real calibration data and, ideally, an empirical comparison on the actual hardware, not inferred from the noiseless simulation alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: The noiseless comparison tells me the theoretical ceiling at each depth, but that's not the whole story for a real deployment — p=2 needs twice as many parameters and real additional two-qubit gates, and every one of those gates has some error probability on real hardware. Before committing to p=2, I'd want the actual calibration data for the target device — real per-gate fidelities, not just a generic range — and I'd want to account for any extra SWAP overhead p=2's circuit needs given that device's connectivity. Then I'd actually run both p=1 and p=2 on the real device, or on a noise model calibrated to it, and compare the real measured approximation ratios side by side, because the theoretical advantage of more depth can get eaten alive by accumulated gate error before it ever shows up in practice. The decision isn't 'more depth is better in principle' — that's already known to be true — it's 'does this specific hardware's noise let that advantage actually materialize,' and that's an empirical question, not something you can answer from the noiseless simulation alone.
questions.example: Noiseless: p=1 -> 0.75, p=2 -> 0.9999 (theoretical ceiling). On real hardware with meaningful gate error accumulated over the extra p=2 gates, the actual measured ratio for p=2 might fall well below 0.9999, potentially even below p=1's real measured result — which can only be known by testing on the actual device.
commonMistakes: Assuming the noiseless simulation result directly predicts real-hardware performance
Committing to higher p purely because the theoretical convergence result says more depth always helps 'in principle'
Not accounting for SWAP/routing overhead's contribution to the real gate count at higher p
keyPoints: The noiseless approximation ratio is a theoretical ceiling, not a real-hardware prediction
Real gate count (including SWAP overhead) and real device calibration data must be factored in
The decision requires empirical testing on the actual target device or a calibrated noise model
The real question is whether noise lets the theoretical depth advantage survive, not whether depth helps in principle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes theoretical noiseless ceiling from real-hardware performance
Proposes gathering real calibration data and accounting for routing overhead
Proposes empirical testing on the real device before committing
Clear, well-reasoned architectural decision process

questions.title: Choosing Between Surface Code and Concatenated Codes at Scale
questions.prompt: You are architecting the error-correction strategy for a fault-tolerant system that must eventually support a large number of logical qubits. The surface code scales as 2d^2-1 physical qubits per logical qubit (quadratic in distance); concatenating the Steane [[7,1,3]] code scales as 7^L (exponential in concatenation level). At small scale, concatenation level 1 (7 qubits) beats even the smallest practical surface code distance (17 qubits at d=3). Design the reasoning for which approach to commit to for a system intended to scale significantly, and identify the specific crossover consideration that should drive the decision.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture decision should be driven by the target scale the system actually needs to reach, not by which approach looks cheaper at the smallest possible instance. At small scale, concatenation's level-1 cost (7 qubits) genuinely beats the surface code's smallest practical distance (17 qubits at d=3) — but this comparison is misleading as a basis for a scaling decision, because the two cost curves have fundamentally different shapes: surface code cost grows quadratically in distance (2d^2-1), while concatenation cost grows exponentially in level (7^L). Exponential curves always eventually overtake quadratic ones, regardless of how favorable the exponential curve's starting point looks — concretely, by concatenation level 4, the cost is already 2,401 qubits, more than a distance-15 surface code's 449 qubits, for error-suppression power that isn't even directly comparable in the same units. The correct architectural approach is to determine the target logical error rate and the number of logical qubits the system must eventually support, project both cost curves out to that target scale (not just the smallest instance), and commit to the surface code specifically because its quadratic growth will dominate favorably at any meaningfully large target scale — this is the real, honest reason the surface code is favored at scale, not because it's cheap in an absolute sense, but because its cost curve's shape wins decisively once you look past the smallest toy case. The crossover consideration specifically to flag: identify the concatenation level and surface-code distance where the two qubit-cost curves intersect, and confirm the system's actual target scale lies well past that crossover point, not near the small-scale region where concatenation still looks attractive.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trap here is judging the two approaches by their cheapest possible instance — concatenation level 1 at 7 qubits does look better than even the smallest useful surface code. But that comparison doesn't tell you anything about which approach to commit to for a system meant to actually scale, because the two cost curves grow completely differently: surface code cost is quadratic in distance, concatenation cost is exponential in level. Exponential curves always catch up to and overtake quadratic ones eventually, no matter how good they look at the start — by level 4, concatenation is already costing more than a distance-15 surface code. So the right way to make this decision is to figure out what logical error rate and how many logical qubits the real system eventually needs, project both cost curves out to that actual target, not the smallest toy case, and commit to the surface code because its curve shape wins decisively once you're past the crossover point — which is exactly where any system intended to scale significantly is going to land.
questions.example: Concatenation: L=1 -> 7 qubits, L=4 -> 2,401 qubits. Surface code: d=3 -> 17 qubits, d=15 -> 449 qubits. By L=4/d=15 scale, concatenation already costs more despite starting much cheaper at L=1/d=3.
commonMistakes: Committing to concatenation because it's cheaper at the smallest instance, without projecting to target scale
Not recognizing that quadratic and exponential growth curves must eventually cross regardless of starting point
Comparing concatenation level and surface-code distance as if they measure error suppression in directly comparable units without caveat
keyPoints: Comparing only the cheapest instance of each code family is misleading for a scaling decision
Surface code cost is quadratic in distance; concatenation cost is exponential in level
Exponential curves always eventually overtake quadratic ones regardless of starting advantage
The decision should be based on projecting both curves to the system's actual target scale, past the crossover point

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the quadratic vs. exponential growth distinction
Correctly explains why the smallest-instance comparison is misleading for a scaling decision
Proposes projecting both curves to the system's actual target scale/crossover point
Clear, well-reasoned architectural conclusion

questions.title: Setting a Shot Budget Architecture From Decision Requirements, Not Round Numbers
questions.prompt: You're designing the shot-budget policy for a production hybrid pipeline that runs 200 tasks per optimization run. The downstream business decision only changes when a measured expectation value crosses a threshold by more than 0.05. Design the shot-budget architecture: how do you derive the actual shot count to use, and what would be architecturally wrong with defaulting to 10,000 shots 'to be thorough'?
questions.modelAnswer: The architecturally correct approach derives the shot count from the actual precision the downstream decision requires, using the relationship that standard error scales as 1/sqrt(shots). If the decision only changes when a value crosses a threshold by more than 0.05, the shot budget should target a standard error comfortably smaller than that threshold (e.g. a standard error around 0.02, well under the 0.05 decision-relevant margin), computed via shots_needed = shots_known * (se_known/target_se)^2 from a known reference point (e.g. 1,000 shots giving standard error ~0.0316). This gives a specific, justified shot count tied directly to what the application needs, rather than an arbitrary round number. Defaulting to 10,000 shots 'to be thorough' is architecturally wrong because it conflates 'more precision is better in isolation' (always true) with 'this specific application needs that much precision' (not established) — given the square-root scaling law, going from a shot count that already meets the 0.05-threshold requirement up to 10,000 shots has a directly computable, often substantial, wasted dollar cost across 200 tasks, for precision the downstream decision will never actually use. The architecture should make the shot count a configuration value derived explicitly from a documented precision requirement (with the decision threshold as an input), not a hardcoded 'safe-sounding' constant, so that any future change to the decision threshold can be traced to a corresponding, justified change in the shot budget.
questions.professionalAnswer: The right way to size this is to work backward from what the decision actually needs: if nothing downstream changes unless the measured value crosses by more than 0.05, I want my standard error comfortably under that — something like 0.02 is a reasonable safety margin without being wasteful — and then use the square-root scaling relationship to compute exactly how many shots that requires from a known reference point. That gives me a specific, justified number, not a guess. Defaulting to 10,000 shots 'to be safe' is the wrong instinct architecturally, because it's treating 'more precision' as free when it isn't — given the square-root law, the jump from whatever shot count actually meets the 0.05 threshold up to 10,000 has a real, computable dollar cost across 200 tasks, paying for precision the business decision will never use. I'd want the shot count to live in configuration, derived explicitly from the decision threshold, so if that threshold ever changes, there's a clear, traceable reason to revisit the shot budget too.
questions.example: A threshold of 0.05 might justify a target standard error of ~0.02, needing roughly 1000*(0.0316/0.02)^2 ≈ 2,500 shots per task — versus 10,000 shots 'to be safe,' a 4x cost difference across 200 tasks for precision the decision doesn't need.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a round, 'sounds thorough' shot count instead of deriving it from the decision threshold
Treating more precision as costless because it's always true in isolation that more precision is better
Hardcoding the shot count rather than making it a traceable, derived configuration value
keyPoints: Shot count should be derived from the downstream decision's actual precision requirement
Use the 1/sqrt(shots) standard-error scaling relationship to compute the minimum justified shot count
Padding shots 'to be safe' has a directly computable, often substantial, wasted dollar cost
The shot budget should be a traceable configuration value tied to the documented decision threshold

Correctly explains why 10,000 shots 'to be safe' is architecturally wrong
Proposes making the shot budget a traceable, derived configuration value

questions.title: Choosing Hardware for a Workload Using Quantum Volume and Beyond
questions.prompt: Device A reports Quantum Volume 128; Device B reports Quantum Volume 64. Your workload needs a circuit that is much wider than it is deep (many qubits, shallow circuit). Design the hardware-selection process: what does the QV comparison actually tell you, and what additional information must you gather before choosing between A and B for this specific workload?
questions.modelAnswer: QV=2^n means the device's largest reliably-passing 'square' circuit (n qubits by n layers) has n=7 for Device A (2^7=128) and n=6 for Device B (2^6=64) — Device A can reliably run a somewhat larger square circuit than Device B, a real and meaningful difference since QV doubles with each step up in n. However, QV is measured using square circuits specifically, and this workload is explicitly not square — it's much wider than deep. A device's QV score says nothing directly about how it handles a wide, shallow circuit, since that circuit's demands on qubit count, connectivity, and gate fidelity differ substantially from a square random circuit's demands. Before choosing between A and B, the architecture process should: (1) check raw qubit count for each device, since a wide circuit's qubit requirement might exceed what QV alone implies about either device's capability; (2) check each device's connectivity graph structure, since a wide circuit's qubit-to-qubit interaction pattern (if any) may route very differently on A vs. B regardless of their QV scores; (3) check speed-oriented benchmarks like CLOPS if the workload involves many repeated circuit executions, since QV says nothing about execution speed; (4) ideally, run the actual workload (or a representative benchmark circuit with a similar width-to-depth ratio) on both devices and compare real measured results, rather than inferring suitability from a composite benchmark built around a different circuit shape entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: QV=2^n tells me Device A's largest reliably-passing square circuit is at n=7, versus n=6 for Device B — a real, meaningful gap given QV doubles per step. But my workload isn't square at all, it's wide and shallow, and QV was specifically built around testing square circuits, so it doesn't directly tell me how either device handles a very different circuit shape. Before I'd pick between them, I'd want to know each device's actual qubit count (since a wide circuit needs enough of them), their connectivity graphs (since that shapes how a wide circuit actually routes), and if this workload runs many times, a speed metric like CLOPS, since QV says nothing about execution speed. Ideally, I'd just run something representative of my actual circuit's shape on both and compare the real results, rather than trusting a benchmark built around a circuit shape that isn't mine.
questions.example: A superconducting device with QV 128 but limited qubit count might be the wrong choice for a wide, 50-qubit-needing circuit, versus a device with QV 64 but 100 available qubits and good connectivity for that specific width.
commonMistakes: Choosing Device A purely because its QV number is higher, without checking if QV's circuit shape matches the workload
Not checking raw qubit count or connectivity separately from the composite QV score
Treating QV as a complete substitute for testing the actual workload on real hardware
keyPoints: QV=2^n: Device A (n=7) can reliably run a larger square circuit than Device B (n=6)
QV is specifically about square circuits and doesn't directly predict wide/shallow circuit performance
Check raw qubit count, connectivity, and speed benchmarks (e.g. CLOPS) relevant to this workload's shape
Ideally, test the actual or representative workload directly on both devices before deciding

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets the QV=2^n comparison between the two devices
Correctly explains why QV doesn't directly predict wide/shallow circuit performance
Lists specific additional data to gather (qubit count, connectivity, speed benchmarks)
Clear, well-reasoned hardware-selection process

questions.title: Designing a Cost Circuit Breaker for a Variational Optimization Loop
questions.prompt: Design a cost circuit breaker for a VQE loop, given that an 8-parameter circuit using parameter-shift gradients needs 17 circuit evaluations per iteration, and a 150-iteration run at 1,000 shots per evaluation on IonQ Aria pricing ($0.30/task + $0.03/shot) costs $77,265 total. Where in the loop does the check belong, what should trigger a halt, and why is tracking spend only in a post-hoc billing dashboard insufficient?
questions.modelAnswer: The circuit breaker must be implemented inside the loop itself, incrementing a running cumulative-spend counter after every circuit evaluation (not just every iteration, since each iteration already makes 17 separate evaluations), using the same cost formula that produces the $77,265 full-run estimate: cost_per_evaluation = $0.30/task + shots*$0.03. The check should trigger a halt (with an alert) whenever cumulative spend crosses a pre-set ceiling — set independently of the iteration-count cap, since optimizers can oscillate, plateau without tripping a tolerance check, or diverge due to a bug, burning through the full iteration budget at real-hardware prices before anyone notices. A post-hoc billing dashboard is insufficient because it only reveals the problem after the money has already been spent — by the time a dashboard shows $77,265 spent, the run is already over and the cost is already sunk; a circuit breaker inside the loop can stop the spend while it's still accruing, at whatever partial-run cost has been reached, rather than letting it run to completion or to the iteration cap regardless of cost. Concretely: track running_cost after each evaluation; if running_cost > cost_ceiling, raise an alert and halt the loop immediately, logging the iteration and evaluation count at which the halt occurred for post-incident review.
questions.professionalAnswer: This has to live inside the loop, checking after every single circuit evaluation, not just once per iteration — since one iteration here is actually 17 separate evaluations, and the dollars add up within an iteration, not just across them. I'd track a running total using the same cost math that gives the $77,265 full-run figure, and set a ceiling that's independent of the max-iteration cap, because the two failure modes are different: an optimizer running out of iterations without converging is one problem, but an optimizer that's broken and just churning indefinitely without ever hitting the iteration cap is a separate, more dangerous problem that only a cost-based check catches. A billing dashboard you check after the fact doesn't help here at all — by the time it shows the spend, the money's already gone. The whole point of a circuit breaker is catching this while it's still happening, so you're out whatever partial cost you'd already accrued, not the full run.
questions.example: cost_per_evaluation = 0.30 + 1000*0.03 = $30.30. After iteration 60 (60*17=1020 evaluations), running_cost ≈ 1020*30.30 ≈ $30,906 — if the ceiling is set at $35,000, the breaker halts here rather than continuing to the full $77,265 at iteration 150.
commonMistakes: Tracking cumulative spend only per-iteration instead of per-evaluation, undercounting mid-iteration cost
Relying on a post-hoc billing dashboard instead of an in-loop check
Tying the cost ceiling to the same control as the max-iteration cap instead of making it an independent check
keyPoints: Cost tracking must happen after every circuit evaluation (17 per iteration here), inside the loop
The ceiling must be an independent check, separate from the max-iteration cap
A post-hoc billing dashboard only reveals cost after it's already been spent
A halting breaker stops partial, not full, cost when something goes wrong

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly places the cost check inside the loop at the per-evaluation level
Correctly specifies an independent ceiling, separate from the iteration cap
Correctly explains why a post-hoc dashboard is insufficient
Clear, concrete architectural design

questions.title: Designing an Orchestration Pipeline That Spans Classical and Quantum Compute
questions.prompt: Design the orchestration architecture for a hybrid pipeline that submits a parameterized circuit to a cloud quantum provider, waits for results, feeds them to a classical optimizer, and repeats. Specify where retry/fallback logic, cost tracking, and the backend abstraction each belong, and how they interact when a job fails mid-run.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture has four layers that must interact cleanly. (1) A backend abstraction layer (submit_circuit, get_result, estimate_cost) isolates the orchestration logic from any specific provider's SDK, so the same orchestration code works across providers via provider-specific adapters. (2) An orchestration layer implements the variational loop itself: build circuit(theta), call backend.submit_circuit(), await the result, compute cost, call the classical optimizer for new theta, check convergence, repeat. (3) A retry/fallback layer wraps every call through the backend abstraction with exponential backoff with jitter (not fixed intervals, to avoid retry storms) and an explicit stopping rule (max attempts and a cumulative-time budget); on exhausting retries, it falls back in order of preference: a different available device, then a classical simulator flagged as lower-fidelity, then an explicit failure returned to the optimizer rather than a silently substituted wrong number. (4) A cost-tracking layer logs every circuit evaluation's cost (including failed, billed retry attempts) against a running total, independent of the iteration-count cap, with a circuit breaker that halts the loop if cumulative spend crosses a pre-set ceiling. When a job fails mid-run: the retry/fallback layer intercepts the failure first (not the orchestration loop directly), attempts backoff-governed retries through the same backend abstraction, and only escalates to a fallback decision or an explicit failure once retries are exhausted — with every attempt, success or failure, logged to the cost-tracking layer so a post-incident review can answer exactly how much the failure and recovery sequence cost and whether a different device or fallback choice would have been cheaper.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into four pieces that each do one job. A backend abstraction (submit, get-result, estimate-cost) so the orchestration code never talks to a specific provider's SDK directly. The orchestration loop itself, which just runs the classic build-circuit, submit, get-result, compute-cost, ask-optimizer-for-next-theta, check-convergence cycle, calling the backend abstraction rather than any specific provider. A retry/fallback layer that wraps every one of those backend calls — exponential backoff with jitter, not fixed intervals, with a clear stopping rule, and a defined fallback order (different device, then simulator, then an explicit failure, never a silently wrong number). And a cost-tracking layer that logs every attempt, including failed ones that got billed, against a running total with its own independent circuit breaker. When something fails mid-run, the retry/fallback layer is what catches it first, not the main loop — it handles backoff and retries through the same backend abstraction, and only once it's truly exhausted does it either fall back or hand an explicit failure back up to the optimizer, with everything logged so the cost side has full visibility into what that failure actually cost.
questions.example: Job fails -> retry layer intercepts -> exponential backoff with jitter -> retry via backend abstraction -> still fails after max attempts -> fallback to a different device -> logged to cost tracker with outcome and cost, independent of whether the loop's main iteration counter advances.
commonMistakes: Putting retry logic directly in the orchestration loop instead of as a separate wrapping layer
Not logging failed/billed retry attempts to the cost tracker
Letting a failure silently substitute a wrong or default value instead of surfacing an explicit failure to the optimizer
keyPoints: Backend abstraction isolates orchestration logic from any specific provider's SDK
Retry/fallback layer wraps backend calls with backoff-with-jitter and a defined fallback order
Cost tracking logs every attempt, including failed ones, against an independent circuit-breaker ceiling
Failures are intercepted by the retry/fallback layer first, never silently substituted with wrong data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the backend abstraction layer's role
Correctly designs the retry/fallback layer and its interaction with the orchestration loop
Correctly designs the cost-tracking layer's integration with the circuit breaker
Clear, coherent overall architecture

questions.title: Designing a Fair Benchmark Pipeline for Quantum vs. Classical Optimization
questions.prompt: You need to design the benchmarking architecture that will compare your QAOA-based portfolio optimizer against a classical baseline before publishing a performance claim. Using the course's four benchmark failure modes, design the measurement pipeline so it avoids all four, specifying exactly what gets timed, what counts as the baseline, and what success criterion applies to both sides.
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline must be designed around full end-to-end timing applied identically to both methods. For the classical side, the baseline must be the strongest classical method reasonably available for the problem class (e.g. simulated annealing or a tuned commercial solver, not an unoptimized greedy search), avoiding the weak-baseline failure mode. For the quantum side, the timed pipeline must include every classical step that's actually part of running QAOA in practice — QUBO construction, Ising conversion, circuit construction, and the full classical parameter-optimizer loop across however many circuit evaluations it takes to converge — not just the 'quantum part,' avoiding the excluded-overhead failure mode. Both sides must be measured on the literal same problem instance (same covariance matrix, same asset set, same constraints) and judged against one shared, explicit success criterion decided in advance (e.g. 'best approximation ratio achieved within X seconds of wall-clock time, evaluated against the known or best-found optimum'), avoiding the mismatched-criteria failure mode. The architecture must report both wall-clock time and iteration/query count, labeled separately, rather than picking whichever framing favors the result, since query count alone can be misleading if each quantum query's real cost differs substantially from a classical iteration's. Finally, the problem sizes tested must be reported explicitly and the pipeline must be run at more than one scale before any claim about how the result generalizes, avoiding the cherry-picked-instance failure mode — a result at a 5-asset scale should never be presented as evidence about a 500-asset scale without separately testing that scale.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this so the four failure modes are structurally impossible to fall into by accident. First, the classical side has to be the real best-available method, not a weak strawman — simulated annealing or a tuned solver, not unoptimized greedy search. Second, the timer on the quantum side starts at QUBO construction and doesn't stop until the classical optimizer loop driving QAOA has actually converged — the 'quantum part alone' is never what gets reported, because that's not what a user would actually experience running this. Third, both methods get the identical problem instance and have to hit the same, explicitly agreed success bar, decided before we run anything — not two different bars quietly compared as if they were the same. Fourth, I'd report wall-clock time and iteration count separately, not pick whichever one looks better, and I'd test more than one problem size before claiming anything about how this generalizes, rather than reporting a nice result from one small, convenient instance and implying it holds at real scale.
questions.example: A published claim that says 'QAOA beat simulated annealing by approximation ratio at equal wall-clock time, tested at 5, 20, and 50 assets, full pipeline timed on both sides' passes all four checks; a claim timing 'just the quantum circuit' against unoptimized greedy search at one small instance fails all four.
commonMistakes: Timing only the quantum circuit execution and excluding the classical optimizer loop's wall-clock cost
Choosing a weak classical baseline to make the comparison look favorable
Testing only one small problem size and implying the result generalizes to realistic scale
keyPoints: Classical baseline must be the strongest reasonably available method, not a weak strawman
Full pipeline timing on the quantum side, including classical optimizer overhead
Same problem instance and one shared, explicit success criterion for both methods
Multiple problem sizes tested and reported, avoiding cherry-picked-instance claims

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs around the weak-baseline failure mode
Correctly designs full end-to-end timing avoiding the excluded-overhead failure mode
Correctly specifies a shared success criterion and same-instance requirement
Correctly addresses testing multiple problem sizes to avoid cherry-picking

questions.title: Designing a Reproducibility Architecture for a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Program
questions.prompt: Design the reproducibility practices that must be built into a quantum-classical hybrid research codebase before any experimental result from it can be trusted or reproduced later. Specifically address random seeds, shot counts, and backend versions, and explain what breaks if any one of these is left unrecorded.
questions.modelAnswer: A reproducible hybrid codebase must record, for every experimental run: (1) the random seed used for both the quantum simulator (e.g. AerSimulator(seed_simulator=...)) and any classical randomness (optimizer initialization, data shuffling), since variational algorithms with random initialization can land on meaningfully different results across seeds, and an unrecorded seed makes a later 'identical' re-run genuinely non-identical; (2) the exact shot count used for every circuit evaluation, since results carry inherent statistical uncertainty (~1/sqrt(shots)) that is only interpretable alongside the shot count that produced it — a result reported without its shot count cannot be judged for statistical significance by anyone reading it later; (3) the backend name and version (e.g. the specific simulator version, or the specific real-hardware backend and its calibration state at run time, as surfaced by name() in the backend abstraction pattern), since the same circuit can produce meaningfully different results on different backend versions or calibration states, and 'IBM hardware' without a specific backend name and approximate calibration date is not a reproducible specification. The architecture should capture all three automatically as part of every run's logged metadata (not relying on a researcher to remember to write them down manually), ideally attached to the result object itself. If any one is left unrecorded: an unrecorded seed means a 'reproduction attempt' might actually be running a different random trajectory and incorrectly concluding the original result doesn't reproduce; an unrecorded shot count means no one can judge whether an observed difference between two results is statistically meaningful or just noise; an unrecorded backend/version means a result might be attributed to an algorithmic effect when it was actually a hardware-calibration-state effect, or vice versa — exactly the kind of confound the course's capstone example ran into with its calibration-window gap.
questions.professionalAnswer: Three things have to be logged automatically with every single run, not remembered after the fact: the random seed (for the simulator and any classical randomness in the optimizer), the exact shot count used, and the specific backend name and version or calibration state. If the seed isn't recorded, someone trying to reproduce the result later might run a genuinely different random trajectory and wrongly conclude the original finding doesn't hold up. If the shot count isn't recorded, nobody — including future-you — can judge whether two different results actually differ meaningfully or are just within each other's statistical noise. And if the backend and its version or calibration state aren't recorded, you can't tell later whether a difference between two runs came from the algorithm or just from running on hardware that had drifted or been recalibrated in between — which is exactly the kind of confound that trips up research results that look surprising but are actually just an artifact of when they were run. All three need to be captured as part of the run's own metadata automatically, not left to a researcher's memory or a lab notebook.
questions.example: A logged run record: {seed: 42, shots: 1024, backend: 'ibm_brisbane', calibration_snapshot: '2026-10-17T14:00Z'} lets a later researcher distinguish 'this result changed because of the algorithm' from 'this result changed because the device drifted between runs.'
commonMistakes: Recording shot count or seed informally in a lab notebook instead of as structured run metadata
Not recording backend calibration state, only the backend's name
Assuming 'we used the same simulator' is a sufficient reproducibility record without the specific version
keyPoints: Random seeds (simulator and classical) must be recorded to make re-runs truly identical
Shot counts must be recorded to judge whether differences are statistically meaningful
Backend name, version, and calibration state must be recorded to rule out hardware-drift confounds
All three should be captured automatically as structured run metadata, not relied on memory

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly specifies recording random seeds and why it matters
Correctly specifies recording shot counts and why it matters
Correctly specifies recording backend/version/calibration state and why it matters
Clear, well-organized architectural recommendation

questions.title: Designing a Multi-SDK Architecture Supporting Both Qiskit and Q#
questions.prompt: Your team needs a single research codebase that can express and run the same algorithm (e.g. Grover's algorithm) using either Qiskit or Q#, chosen at configuration time, without duplicating algorithm logic for each SDK. Design the architecture, and identify the specific design-philosophy difference between the two languages that makes this harder than it looks.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture should separate 'what algorithm to run, at what abstract level' from 'how it's expressed in a specific SDK's syntax and execution model.' A thin abstraction layer defines the algorithm's structural parameters generically (e.g. for Grover's: the oracle definition, the number of qubits, the iteration count) and delegates actual circuit construction and execution to an SDK-specific adapter chosen by configuration — a QiskitGroverAdapter building a QuantumCircuit with explicit H/CZ/diffuser gates and running it via a Qiskit backend, and a QSharpGroverAdapter calling into a compiled Q# operation (via the qsharp Python package or a Q# project) with equivalent structure. The specific design-philosophy difference that makes this harder than a simple wrapper: Qiskit's circuit model is explicit and imperative — you build a specific gate sequence, including explicitly writing out any 'undo' gates for something like a diffuser. Q#'s operation model is declarative with respect to inversion and control — operations declared 'is Adj + Ctl' let the compiler automatically derive their adjoint and controlled forms, and constructs like within/apply express a wrap-act-unwrap pattern without the programmer writing the unwrap half by hand. This means a direct line-by-line translation between the two SDKs' implementations of the same algorithm will diverge structurally even when functionally equivalent, so the shared abstraction layer must operate at the level of 'what structural steps does this algorithm need' (oracle, diffuser, iteration count) rather than 'what exact gate sequence,' letting each SDK-specific adapter implement those steps in its own idiomatic way rather than forcing one SDK's structural style onto the other.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key design move is separating the algorithm's abstract shape — for Grover's, that's 'what's the oracle, how many qubits, how many iterations' — from how that shape actually gets expressed in a given SDK. So I'd have one adapter per SDK, each building the equivalent circuit in its own idiomatic way, with a shared interface describing the algorithm at the structural level rather than the exact gate-by-gate level. The reason this is trickier than it sounds is that Qiskit and Q# have genuinely different philosophies: Qiskit makes you write out every gate explicitly, including the 'undo' half of something like a diffuser, while Q# lets you declare an operation as invertible and controllable and have the compiler derive those forms automatically, using patterns like within/apply that only need the 'forward' half written out. If I tried to force a literal, gate-by-gate translation between the two, I'd end up fighting each language's own idioms instead of using them — so the shared abstraction has to live one level up, at 'what structural pieces does this algorithm need,' not 'what exact gates.'
questions.example: QiskitGroverAdapter.build_diffuser() writes out H, X, CZ, X, H explicitly. QSharpGroverAdapter's Diffuser operation is declared 'is Adj + Ctl' and uses within/apply, letting the compiler derive the closing half automatically — functionally equivalent, structurally very different code.
commonMistakes: Attempting a literal, gate-by-gate translation between the two SDKs instead of a structural abstraction
Not identifying the declarative Adj/Ctl derivation as the specific philosophical difference that matters here
Designing the shared interface at too low a level, forcing one SDK's style onto the other
keyPoints: Separate the algorithm's abstract structural parameters from each SDK's specific expression of them
Use one adapter per SDK, chosen by configuration, each implementing the structure idiomatically
Qiskit's explicit, imperative gate style contrasts with Q#'s declarative Adj/Ctl derivation
The shared abstraction layer must operate at the structural level, not the exact-gate-sequence level

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs a structural abstraction with per-SDK adapters
Correctly identifies the Qiskit-explicit vs. Q#-declarative design-philosophy difference
Explains why a literal translation approach would fail
Clear, well-organized architectural design

questions.title: Choosing an Error-Mitigation Strategy for a Production Measurement Pipeline
questions.prompt: You must choose between readout error mitigation and zero-noise extrapolation (or both) for a production pipeline measuring expectation values on real hardware. Design the decision process: what does each technique actually correct, and under what circumstances would you architect the pipeline to use both together rather than either alone?
questions.modelAnswer: Readout error mitigation corrects a specific, known distortion introduced at the measurement step itself — the probability of reading a qubit's true 0 as a 1 or vice versa — and is typically characterized by a calibration matrix built from known reference circuits, then inverted/applied to correct observed counts after the fact. Zero-noise extrapolation addresses a different source entirely: error that accumulates during the circuit's execution from imperfect gates, which cannot be characterized by a fixed calibration matrix the way readout error can, and instead requires deliberately running the circuit at amplified noise levels and extrapolating back to the unreachable zero-noise point. Because these two techniques target different error sources (measurement-step distortion vs. gate-accumulated error), they are not competing alternatives — the architecturally correct default for a production pipeline is to apply both together: readout error mitigation as a relatively cheap, well-characterized correction applied to every measurement, and ZNE (via gate folding and extrapolation, or production tooling like mitiq or qiskit-ibm-runtime's resilience_level) layered on top to address gate-accumulated noise, since neither technique corrects the error the other is designed for. The one circumstance to architect for choosing ZNE alone or neither: if the circuit is short enough or the measurement step dominates total error, the marginal benefit of ZNE's extra circuit evaluations (gate-folded runs at multiple noise scales, multiplying the total shot/cost budget) may not be worth it relative to just applying the cheaper readout correction — this should be an explicit cost-benefit decision made per-workload, not a default assumption that 'more mitigation is always worth it.'
questions.professionalAnswer: These two aren't really alternatives to each other — they fix different problems. Readout error mitigation is specifically about the measurement step: the chance of reading a 0 as a 1 or vice versa, which you can characterize with a calibration matrix and correct after the fact, pretty cheaply. Zero-noise extrapolation is about everything that goes wrong during the circuit itself from imperfect gates, which you can't fix with a calibration matrix — you have to deliberately run the circuit noisier on purpose, at a few different noise levels, and extrapolate back to what zero noise would have given you. Since they're fixing different things, my default for a production pipeline is to run both together: readout mitigation because it's cheap and well-understood, plus ZNE layered on top for the gate-accumulated error neither technique alone would catch. The one place I'd reconsider is if the circuit is short enough that gate error barely matters relative to readout error — ZNE costs real extra circuit evaluations at multiple noise scales, so if it's not buying much, that's a legitimate reason to skip it for that specific workload, but that should be a deliberate cost-benefit call, not an assumption.
questions.example: A deep variational circuit on a device with modest readout error but meaningful gate error benefits from both: readout mitigation correcting the measurement step, ZNE correcting the accumulated gate noise from the circuit's depth.
commonMistakes: Treating readout mitigation and ZNE as competing alternatives rather than complementary corrections
Applying ZNE by default without weighing its extra circuit-evaluation cost against the workload's actual gate-error exposure
Not identifying that readout mitigation addresses measurement-step error specifically, distinct from gate-accumulated error
keyPoints: Readout mitigation corrects measurement-step bit-flip distortion via a calibration matrix
ZNE corrects gate-accumulated error via deliberate noise amplification and extrapolation
The two target different error sources and are complementary, not competing
Combining both is the sensible production default; skipping ZNE is a deliberate cost-benefit call for short circuits

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes what each technique actually corrects
Correctly argues they are complementary rather than alternatives
Identifies a reasonable circumstance for skipping ZNE as a cost-benefit decision
Clear, well-reasoned architectural decision
