questions.title: Architecting a Pipeline That Scales a Portfolio QUBO Honestly
questions.prompt: Your 3-asset portfolio QUBO formulation works cleanly, but the business wants this scaled to a real portfolio of 500 assets using QAOA. Design the architecture for how you'd approach this scale-up, and specifically address what honest technical constraints you must surface to the business before committing to a quantum-hardware-based solution at this scale.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture must separate the QUBO formulation step (which scales cleanly — the mean-variance objective and budget-penalty structure generalize directly from 3 to 500 assets, just with a larger covariance matrix and Q matrix) from the quantum execution step (which does not scale cleanly at all). At 500 assets, a direct one-qubit-per-asset QAOA encoding would need 500 qubits of good, well-connected quality — far beyond current NISQ hardware's practical reach for a circuit this deep, and even before considering the SWAP/routing overhead a dense covariance structure would impose on any realistically connected device. The honest architecture for this request routes the formulation through the same QUBO/Ising pipeline validated at small scale, but executes it using a classical QUBO solver (simulated annealing, or a quantum-inspired classical solver) as the actual production backend at this scale, with QAOA reserved for a clearly-labeled research/benchmarking track run on small subsets (e.g. 10-20 assets) to measure whether any quantum approach shows a real, benchmarked advantage over the classical solver on the same instances — never presented as the production solution for the full 500-asset problem today. The specific honest constraints to surface to the business before committing to a quantum-hardware-based production solution: current hardware's qubit count and connectivity cannot run a 500-qubit QAOA circuit with usable fidelity today; even if it could, no benchmarked result in the field currently shows QAOA beating a well-tuned classical solver like simulated annealing at this kind of problem size; and the honest recommendation is a classical-solver production path now, with quantum explored as a monitored research track, not a committed delivery dependency.
questions.professionalAnswer: The formulation side scales fine — the QUBO math for 500 assets is the same shape as for 3, just a bigger matrix. The part that doesn't scale is running that QUBO through QAOA on real hardware: 500 qubits of usable quality, with the connectivity a dense covariance matrix would demand, is well beyond what current hardware can actually deliver reliably today. So the architecture I'd propose is: use the validated QUBO/Ising pipeline, but have the actual production solver be a classical method — simulated annealing or a comparable classical QUBO solver — and keep QAOA as a clearly separate research track, tested on small subsets like 10-20 assets, specifically to see if it shows any real, fairly-benchmarked advantage over the classical solver at that smaller scale. What I'd tell the business directly, before they commit to anything quantum-hardware-based here: today's hardware can't run a circuit this size reliably, nobody in the field has shown QAOA beating a good classical solver at this kind of scale yet, and the responsible path is classical in production now, with quantum as a monitored side investigation, not something the delivery timeline depends on.
questions.example: Production: classical simulated-annealing solver running the full 500-asset QUBO today. Research track: QAOA benchmarked against the same classical solver on 10-20-asset subsets of the same real covariance data, reported honestly either way.
commonMistakes: Committing to a QAOA-based production solution for 500 assets without surfacing the hardware feasibility gap
Not separating the QUBO formulation (which scales) from the quantum execution (which does not)
Presenting quantum optimization as production-ready without a benchmarked result showing an actual advantage
keyPoints: QUBO formulation scales cleanly from 3 to 500 assets; quantum execution does not
500 qubits of usable quality and connectivity is beyond current NISQ hardware's practical reach
No benchmarked result currently shows QAOA beating a tuned classical solver at this scale
Honest architecture: classical solver in production, QAOA as a monitored research track on small subsets

Correctly identifies the hardware feasibility gap at 500 qubits
Proposes a classical-production/quantum-research-track architecture
Clearly articulates the honest constraints to surface to the business

questions.title: Designing Connectivity-Aware Circuit Architecture to Minimize Routing Overhead
questions.prompt: You're architecting a circuit-compilation pipeline that will run many QAOA circuits with dense, all-to-all cost-Hamiltonian interactions on a sparsely-connected superconducting device. Design the architecture decisions that minimize SWAP-driven routing overhead, and explain how you would validate that your chosen approach actually reduces total error versus a naive compilation.
questions.modelAnswer: Three architecture decisions reduce routing overhead for dense interaction patterns on sparse hardware. First, qubit placement: rather than accepting the compiler's default initial layout, run a placement step that analyzes the circuit's full interaction graph (which pairs of logical qubits need two-qubit gates) against the device's actual connectivity graph, and chooses an initial logical-to-physical mapping that minimizes the number of required long-range interactions before any routing even begins — this is a one-time analysis per problem structure that pays off across every circuit sharing that structure. Second, routing: use the compiler's heuristic router (e.g. Qiskit's SabreSwap or a comparable heuristic) at a higher optimization level, and run it multiple times with different random seeds, keeping the lowest-SWAP-count result found, since heuristic routers are not guaranteed optimal and can produce meaningfully different SWAP counts across runs. Third, for QAOA specifically, consider whether the cost Hamiltonian's dense interaction structure can be restructured (e.g. reordering which ZZ-interaction terms are applied in which layer) to reduce the number of simultaneous long-range interactions needed, rather than treating the Hamiltonian's term ordering as fixed. To validate the approach actually reduces total error: compile the same circuit both the naive way (default layout, single routing pass) and the optimized way, count the total two-qubit gate count (native + SWAP-derived) for each, and using the device's actual per-gate error rate, compute the estimated total error probability for both versions — directly comparable to the course's verified example (40 native + 20 SWAPs = 100 total ops, ~39% error vs. the lower overhead of an optimized mapping) — and, where possible, run both versions on the real device or a calibrated noise model and compare actual measured output fidelity, not just the gate-count estimate alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: For a dense interaction pattern on sparse hardware, I'd focus on three things. First, don't accept whatever initial qubit layout the compiler defaults to — analyze the circuit's actual interaction graph against the device's real connectivity and choose a starting placement that minimizes long-range interactions before any SWAP routing even starts. Second, don't settle for one routing pass either — run the heuristic router multiple times with different seeds and keep whichever result inserts the fewest SWAPs, since these heuristics aren't guaranteed to find the best answer on the first try. Third, for QAOA specifically, it's worth asking whether the order you apply the cost Hamiltonian's interaction terms in is actually fixed, or whether restructuring that order could reduce how many long-range interactions are needed at once. To actually validate this is working, I'd compile the same circuit the naive way and the optimized way, count total two-qubit gates for each, and use the device's real per-gate error rate to estimate total error probability for both — and ideally run both on the actual device and compare measured fidelity directly, not just trust the gate-count estimate on its own.
questions.example: Naive compilation: 40 native gates + 35 SWAPs (105 CNOT-equivalents) at 0.5% error -> high total error probability. Optimized placement + multi-seed routing: 40 native gates + 12 SWAPs (36 CNOT-equivalents) -> substantially lower total error probability, confirmed by comparing measured fidelity on the real device.
commonMistakes: Accepting the compiler's default layout and single routing pass without optimization
Treating the cost Hamiltonian's term ordering as immutable rather than a lever for reducing interaction density
Validating only via gate-count estimates without confirming on real hardware or a calibrated noise model
keyPoints: Analyze the circuit's interaction graph against device connectivity before choosing initial qubit placement
Run the heuristic router multiple times/seeds and keep the lowest-SWAP-count result
Consider restructuring the Hamiltonian term ordering to reduce simultaneous long-range interactions
Validate by comparing gate counts and, ideally, real measured fidelity between naive and optimized compilation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes connectivity-aware qubit placement as a key architecture decision
Proposes multi-seed/optimized routing as a key architecture decision
Proposes Hamiltonian-structure-aware restructuring as an additional lever
Describes a concrete validation method comparing naive vs. optimized compilation

questions.title: Designing a Hybrid Workflow's Latency and Shot Budget Together
questions.prompt: You're architecting a hybrid workflow where each optimization iteration has a hard latency budget (the result must arrive within a fixed window to remain useful downstream) and a cost budget (shot count directly trades cost for precision). Design how these two budgets interact architecturally, including what happens when a queued job's expected wait time threatens the latency budget.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture must treat the latency budget and the shot/cost budget as two independent constraints feeding into the same per-iteration decision, not a single combined number. Before submitting each job, the orchestration layer should check the current queue's estimated wait time against the remaining latency budget for that iteration (tracked as a cumulative-time budget across the retry/backoff logic, per the retry-and-fallback architecture); if the estimated wait alone threatens to exceed the latency budget, the architecture should trigger the same fallback decision tree used for exhausted retries — first, check a different, available device with a shorter queue (preserving the full, precise shot count); if no device can meet the latency budget, fall back to a classical simulator for this iteration, clearly flagged as a lower-fidelity substitute, which trades result accuracy for guaranteed speed; only as a last resort should the iteration fail explicitly, letting the calling optimizer decide how to handle a missing data point, rather than silently returning a late or low-shot-count result that might distort the optimization trajectory. Separately, the shot count itself should be set from the precision the downstream decision actually needs (per the shot-budget cost/accuracy framework), not inflated or deflated based on latency pressure — conflating 'reduce shots to go faster' with the queue-wait problem risks quietly degrading result quality as a hidden side effect of a timing problem, when the real fix for a timing problem is a device or fallback decision, not a shot-count cut. Every one of these decisions — queue-wait check, device switch, simulator fallback, explicit failure — should be logged with its cost and latency outcome, feeding the same cost-tracking dashboard used elsewhere in the pipeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep these as two separate checks feeding the same decision point, rather than merging them into one number. Before a job goes out, check the queue's estimated wait against whatever latency budget is left for this iteration. If that alone is going to blow the budget, I'd reach for the same fallback ladder used for exhausted retries: try a different device with a shorter queue first, keeping the full shot count and precision intact; if nothing can meet the latency window, fall back to a classical simulator for just this iteration, clearly flagged as lower-fidelity; and only if neither works, fail the iteration explicitly rather than quietly returning something late or degraded. What I'd specifically avoid is reaching for 'just cut the shot count to go faster' as the fix for a timing problem — the shot count should be set by what precision the downstream decision needs, full stop; using it as a timing lever quietly trades away result quality to solve a problem that's really about device availability, not statistics. Every one of these fallback decisions gets logged with its cost and timing outcome into the same tracking the rest of the pipeline uses.
questions.example: Iteration's latency budget: 90 seconds remaining. Primary device's estimated queue wait: 150 seconds (exceeds budget) -> check alternate device: 40 seconds (fits) -> submit there, full shot count preserved, latency budget met without touching precision.
commonMistakes: Reducing shot count as a quick fix for a queue-wait/latency problem instead of switching devices or falling back
Treating latency and cost budgets as one combined constraint instead of two independent checks
Not logging fallback decisions triggered by latency pressure into the same cost-tracking system
keyPoints: Latency budget and shot/cost budget are independent constraints, checked separately per iteration
A threatened latency budget triggers the same fallback ladder as exhausted retries: alternate device, then simulator, then explicit failure
Shot count should be set by precision needs, never used as a lever to solve a timing problem
All fallback decisions, including latency-driven ones, should be logged to the same cost/outcome tracking

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly treats latency and shot/cost budgets as independent constraints
Correctly designs the fallback ladder triggered by a threatened latency budget
Correctly argues against using shot count as a latency-fix lever
Clear, well-organized architectural design

questions.title: Resisting the Urge to Reframe a Hypothesis After Seeing the Data
questions.prompt: Your capstone's written proposal predicted that zero-noise extrapolation's fidelity improvement would be smaller at 5 qubits than at 3 qubits. Your actual data shows the opposite. Describe how you would handle writing up this result, specifically addressing the temptation to quietly revise your stated hypothesis to match what you found.
questions.modelAnswer: I would report the result exactly as it contradicts the original prediction, referring back explicitly to my dated, written Lesson 12 proposal as the record of what I predicted before seeing this data, rather than quietly deciding after the fact that I'd 'really' expected the opposite — a practice known as HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known), which is a well-documented and genuinely dishonest research failure mode. Before concluding the hypothesis itself was simply wrong, I would apply the standard discrepancy-diagnosis checklist: rule out implementation bugs and parameter mismatches first, then check whether the two conditions were actually run under comparable device states (e.g. the same calibration window). If that check reveals a confound, like the two qubit-count conditions running six hours apart across a device recalibration, the honest conclusion is that the relative-magnitude claim wasn't fairly tested under these specific run conditions, not that the underlying mechanism was definitively disproven. I would state this precisely in the final report: the direction-of-effect claim remains supported, the relative-magnitude claim is not supported under these conditions, and the calibration-window gap is named explicitly in the limitations section as the likely confound — giving the reader everything they need to judge the result's actual scope, rather than either hiding the contradiction or overclaiming that it disproves the proposed mechanism.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core discipline here is referring back to what I actually wrote down before I had the data, not what I'd now prefer I'd predicted. My dated proposal is the record, and I'd report the real result against it honestly — including the part where it didn't go the way I expected. Before jumping to 'my hypothesis was wrong,' I'd go through the discrepancy checklist: rule out a bug, rule out a parameter mismatch, and specifically check whether both conditions ran under comparable device states, since a calibration gap between them is exactly the kind of confound that could produce this. If I find that gap, I'd say so plainly in the report — the direction of the effect still held, the magnitude comparison didn't hold up under these specific conditions, and here's the likely reason why — rather than either burying the contradiction or quietly rewriting my hypothesis to pretend I saw it coming.
questions.example: Lesson 12 proposal (dated, before data): 'the 5-qubit mitigation improvement will be smaller than the 3-qubit one.' Actual result: 5-qubit improvement (0.160) slightly larger than 3-qubit (0.155). Final report: states this contradiction explicitly, diagnoses the calibration-window confound, and does not retroactively rewrite the original prediction.
commonMistakes: Quietly rewriting the stated hypothesis after the fact to match the observed data (HARKing)
Concluding the hypothesis was definitively wrong without first checking for a design/execution confound
Hiding or downplaying the contradiction rather than naming it explicitly in the report
keyPoints: Refer back to the dated, written proposal as the honest record of the original prediction
HARKing (rewriting a hypothesis after seeing results) is a recognized, dishonest research failure mode
Apply the discrepancy checklist (bugs, parameter mismatches, design/execution confounds) before concluding
Report the contradiction explicitly, including the direction-of-effect claim that still held

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explicitly identifies and avoids the HARKing failure mode
Describes applying the discrepancy-diagnosis checklist before concluding
Describes honest, precise reporting of what was and wasn't supported
Clear, well-reasoned communication of the approach

questions.title: Scoping a Capstone Project You Know Is at Risk of Overrunning
questions.prompt: You're proposing a capstone comparing zero-noise-extrapolation results across 3-qubit and 5-qubit GHZ states on real cloud quantum hardware. Describe how you would build a 'cut list' into your proposal before starting, and walk through what you'd actually cut first if time ran short, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: I would write an explicit, ordered cut list before starting any experimental work, deciding now what gets dropped first under time pressure rather than improvising later when I'm already under pressure. For this specific proposal, the core, must-finish deliverable is the 3-qubit reproduction — it's the smallest, best-specified piece, with clear prior literature to compare against and already-flagged risks. The 5-qubit extension is the first thing on the cut list, specifically because it's the piece added on top of an already-working core, which is exactly the right place to absorb a schedule slip without threatening the core deliverable at all. If time is very short, I'd drop the 5-qubit extension entirely and report the 3-qubit reproduction alone, honestly framed as a reproduction-only deliverable, not something that silently disappeared with no explanation. If time is moderately short, I'd keep both qubit counts but reduce the shot count per condition, trading some precision for completing both comparisons. If time allows, I'd treat a third qubit count as a bonus, never a requirement. Having this decided in advance means a real time crunch becomes 'execute step 1 of the plan I already wrote,' not a stressful scramble to figure out what to sacrifice while the clock is already running.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I start any actual experiments, I write down, in order, exactly what I'll drop first if time gets tight — deciding that now, while I'm not under pressure, instead of improvising later when I am. For this project, the 3-qubit reproduction is the must-finish core: it's well-specified, has real literature to compare against, and the risks are already known. The 5-qubit extension goes first on the cut list, precisely because it's additional work layered on top of a working core — that's exactly the kind of thing you want to be able to drop without threatening the deliverable itself. If things get really tight, I report the 3-qubit result alone, clearly labeled as a reproduction, not quietly omit the comparison and hope nobody notices. If it's only moderately tight, I'd rather cut shot count per condition than cut a whole qubit-count comparison. And if I actually have time to spare, a third qubit count becomes a bonus, not something I'd ever have promised upfront. The whole point of deciding this order in advance is that a crunch just becomes following the plan, not a last-minute scramble.
questions.example: Cut list, in order: (1) drop the 5-qubit extension, report 3-qubit reproduction alone if time is very short; (2) keep both qubit counts but reduce shot count if moderately short; (3) add a third qubit count only as a bonus if time allows.
commonMistakes: Not writing the cut list down before starting, leaving scope decisions to be improvised under pressure later
Cutting the core reproduction deliverable instead of the extension layered on top of it
Silently dropping scope without honestly reframing the deliverable's actual coverage in the final report
keyPoints: A cut list is written and ordered before experimental work starts, not improvised later
The core, well-specified deliverable (3-qubit reproduction) is protected; the extension is cut first
Cutting scope should be paired with honest reframing of the deliverable, not silent omission
Having the list pre-decided turns a time crunch into executing a known plan, not a scramble

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes writing an explicit, ordered cut list before starting work
Correctly protects the core deliverable and cuts the extension first
Emphasizes honest reframing of scope rather than silent omission
Clear, well-organized explanation

questions.title: Asking a Peer Reviewer for Useful Feedback on Your Capstone Report
questions.prompt: You're about to ask a colleague to review your capstone report before you finalize it. Describe specifically what you would ask them, and why a vague request like 'can you look this over?' would get you worse feedback than what you're planning to ask instead.
questions.modelAnswer: I would ask specific, pointed questions rather than a generic request, because naming the exact thing I want checked gets me a specific, actionable answer instead of generic, hard-to-act-on comments. I'd ask: 'Does my methods section give you enough detail that you could attempt to replicate this experiment yourself?' — which directly tests whether my write-up has the specificity a reproducible methods section needs, not just whether it reads smoothly. I'd ask: 'Does my conclusion claim anything my results don't actually support?' — which tests scoping discipline specifically, since it's easy for a conclusion to drift slightly broader than the evidence over multiple drafts without the author noticing. And I'd ask: 'Is there anywhere you got confused or had to re-read a sentence?' — which catches clarity problems that are genuinely hard to see in your own familiar writing, since you already know what you meant and can't easily read it as a stranger would. A generic 'can you look this over?' produces generic feedback like 'looks good' or vague stylistic comments, because the reviewer has no specific target to check against and will default to whatever catches their eye rather than systematically verifying the things that actually matter for a research report's integrity.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask three specific things instead of a vague 'take a look.' First: 'could you actually replicate this from my methods section alone?' — that's testing something concrete, not just readability. Second: 'does my conclusion claim anything the results don't actually back up?' — because conclusions have a way of drifting slightly broader than the evidence without the author ever noticing it happen across drafts. Third: 'where did you get confused or have to re-read something?' — because I genuinely can't see my own writing's confusing spots the way a fresh reader can, since I already know what I meant. The reason a vague 'can you look this over?' gets worse feedback is that it gives the reviewer nothing specific to check against, so they end up either saying something generically positive or commenting on whatever happens to catch their eye, instead of systematically testing the things that actually matter — replicability, scope accuracy, and clarity.
questions.example: Vague request result: 'looks good, maybe tighten the intro.' Specific request result: 'I couldn't tell from your methods section what shot count you used for the 5-qubit runs — that would block someone trying to replicate this,' and 'your conclusion says mitigation significantly helps, but I don't see a significance test in your results section.'
commonMistakes: Asking a vague 'can you look this over?' and expecting specific, actionable feedback anyway
Not asking about replicability specifically, missing gaps a careful reviewer would otherwise catch
Assuming clarity issues in your own writing are visible to you without a fresh reader's perspective
keyPoints: Specific requests produce specific, actionable feedback; vague requests produce vague feedback
Ask whether the methods section would actually support independent replication
Ask whether the conclusion claims anything the results don't actually support
Ask where the reviewer got confused, since clarity gaps are hard to see in your own writing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes specific, targeted review questions rather than a vague request
Correctly explains why specificity produces more actionable feedback
Covers replicability, scope/conclusion accuracy, and clarity as distinct review targets
Clear, well-organized explanation

questions.title: Triaging a Reviewer Comment About an Unsupported 'Significantly' Claim
questions.prompt: A peer reviewer tells you: 'Your conclusion says mitigation significantly helps, but I don't see a significance test anywhere in your results section.' Using the must-fix / worth-considering / noted-but-not-changing triage categories, which category does this belong in, and what specific action would you take?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a must-fix comment, not worth-considering or noted-but-not-changing. It identifies a genuine, specific unsupported claim — using the word 'significantly' implies a statistical significance test was run and passed, and if no such test actually appears in the results section, the conclusion is overclaiming relative to the evidence actually presented, which is exactly the kind of gap a careful reader shouldn't have to go looking for. This isn't a stylistic preference I could reasonably disagree with and set aside; it's a factual mismatch between what the conclusion asserts and what the results section demonstrates. The specific action: either (a) go back and actually run the appropriate significance test on the existing data (e.g. comparing the measured effect against the standard error of the measurements, given the shot-noise considerations from the course) and, if it passes, cite the test explicitly in the results section before the conclusion uses the word 'significantly'; or (b) if no such test was run and there isn't time to run one properly, revise the conclusion's language to something accurate and not overclaiming, such as 'mitigation showed a measurable improvement at both qubit counts' rather than 'significantly helps,' until a proper test is actually in place to support the stronger word.
questions.professionalAnswer: That one's a must-fix, no question. The reviewer caught something real and specific — I used the word 'significantly,' which implies an actual statistical test backs that claim, and if that test isn't in my results section, my conclusion is saying something my evidence doesn't actually support yet. That's not a style note I could reasonably push back on; it's a factual gap between what I claimed and what I showed. So my action is one of two things: either go run the actual significance test against the data I already have and cite it explicitly before I use that word, or, if I don't have time to do that properly, just soften the conclusion's language to something the evidence does support — 'showed a measurable improvement' instead of 'significantly helps' — until I actually have a test in place that earns the stronger word.
questions.example: Before: 'Mitigation significantly improves fidelity at both qubit counts.' After (if no test run): 'Mitigation showed a measurable fidelity improvement at both qubit counts (0.155 and 0.160 reduction in error rate).' After (if test run and passes): same sentence, now with the specific test and result cited in the results section.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a style preference (worth-considering) rather than a factual accuracy gap (must-fix)
Leaving the word 'significantly' unchanged without either running a test or softening the claim
Dismissing the comment as pedantic instead of recognizing the real scoping discipline issue it raises
keyPoints: This is a must-fix comment: a factual mismatch between claim and evidence, not a style preference
Using 'significantly' without a cited significance test is a genuine overclaim
The fix is either running and citing the appropriate test, or softening the conclusion's language
Feedback triage should distinguish factual accuracy issues from stylistic or scope-based disagreements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly classifies this as a must-fix comment
Correctly explains why this is a factual overclaim, not a style issue
Proposes a concrete, specific fix (run and cite a test, or soften the language)
Clear, well-reasoned explanation

questions.title: Presenting a Noisy-Hardware Result to a Non-Specialist Stakeholder
questions.prompt: You need to present your zero-noise-extrapolation results to a product team with no quantum computing background, who will decide whether to continue funding this research direction. Describe how you would structure the talk, and give a plain-language translation of: 'Richardson extrapolation across five noise-scaling factors estimated the zero-noise limit of the measured GHZ fidelity.'
questions.modelAnswer: I would structure the talk around six elements, not as a simplified version of the technical talk but as a genuinely different structure built for this audience: (1) the real-world stakes in one sentence — why anyone outside the field should care that quantum hardware is noisy and correction techniques are being developed; (2) a concrete, visualizable analogy for the core concept, such as a blurry photo and a sharpening filter for error mitigation; (3) what was actually done, in plain language, without circuit diagrams or equations; (4) what was found, with the actual numbers translated into accessible framing (percentages, 'cut errors by about two-thirds,' not raw technical units); (5) honest caveats stated in plain language, such as 'this was tested on one device at two circuit sizes, so we can't yet say this pattern holds everywhere'; (6) why it matters going forward, connecting back to the stakes from step 1. For the specific sentence: 'Richardson extrapolation across five noise-scaling factors estimated the zero-noise limit of the measured GHZ fidelity' translates to something like: 'We ran the same test circuit at five different, deliberately increased noise levels, then used that pattern to estimate what the result would have looked like if the hardware had no noise at all — even though we can never actually run it with zero noise directly.' This keeps the real meaning intact (multiple noise levels, a mathematical extrapolation technique, estimating an unreachable ideal point) without using jargon the audience can't evaluate, and without overstating certainty the result doesn't have.
questions.professionalAnswer: For this audience, I wouldn't just strip jargon out of my technical talk — I'd build it around a different structure entirely: start with why this matters in plain terms, give one concrete analogy they can picture, explain what we actually did without equations or circuit diagrams, give the real numbers but translated into something they have a reference point for, state the honest limits of what we tested in plain language, and circle back to why it matters. For that specific sentence, I'd say something like: 'we deliberately ran the same test five times at increasingly higher noise levels, then used the pattern in how the result got worse to estimate what it would have looked like with no noise at all — since we can never actually turn the noise all the way off on real hardware.' That keeps everything true — five data points, a mathematical estimation technique, an unreachable ideal — just without the jargon this audience has no way to independently evaluate.
questions.example: Jargon: 'GHZ state fidelity.' Plain: 'how closely the hardware's actual output matched the known correct answer for a standard test circuit.' Jargon: 'shots.' Plain: 'repeated measurements, like flipping a coin many times instead of once, so we can trust the measured probability instead of one lucky or unlucky result.'
commonMistakes: Treating the non-specialist talk as the technical talk with jargon simply deleted, losing accuracy
Omitting honest caveats because they feel too technical to translate
Overselling the result to an audience that can't independently check the claim
keyPoints: The structure for a non-specialist talk is genuinely different, not a simplified technical talk
Replace jargon with accurate, visualizable plain language, without losing precision
Translate actual numbers into accessible framing rather than dropping them
State honest caveats in plain language, resisting the temptation to oversell to an audience that can't check the claim

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a complete, appropriate non-specialist talk structure
Provides an accurate, non-misleading plain-language translation of the given sentence
Addresses honest caveats and avoiding overselling
Clear, well-organized explanation

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Manager's Premature 'Quantum Breakthrough' Announcement
questions.prompt: Your manager wants to announce your QAOA portfolio-optimization result (approximation ratio 0.9999 at depth p=2 on a 4-asset toy problem) to the wider company as a 'quantum breakthrough in portfolio optimization.' How would you handle this conversation, balancing honesty about the real limits of the result against not undermining your manager or the team's work?
questions.modelAnswer: I would approach this as a collaborative correction, not a confrontation, framing it around protecting the team's credibility rather than just being technically pedantic. I would acknowledge the real, genuine achievement first — getting from a 0.75 to a 0.9999 approximation ratio by adding one layer is a legitimate, interesting result worth sharing — and then clearly separate what's actually been shown from what 'quantum breakthrough in portfolio optimization' would imply to a general audience. Specifically, I'd point out: this result is on a 4-asset toy problem, not a realistic portfolio size (real portfolios have tens to thousands of assets); there's no benchmarked comparison here against a strong classical baseline like simulated annealing, so there's no basis yet for a claim that quantum beats classical at this task; and the honest framing, consistent with how the course's own fair-benchmarking discipline would evaluate this claim, is something like 'we demonstrated that increasing QAOA depth meaningfully improves solution quality on a small benchmark problem — a promising, concrete result worth continuing to investigate' rather than 'a breakthrough.' I would propose this reframed language directly, emphasizing that an overclaimed announcement risks real reputational damage if a technically literate audience (or a competitor, or a journalist) points out the gap between 'breakthrough' and 'improved approximation ratio on a 4-node toy graph,' which protects the team's credibility rather than undermining it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by actually crediting the real result — going from 75% to effectively 100% approximation ratio by adding one more layer is genuinely interesting and worth telling people about. Then I'd walk through, specifically, why 'breakthrough in portfolio optimization' oversells it: this is a 4-asset toy problem, nowhere near what a real portfolio looks like, and we haven't actually benchmarked this against a strong classical method like simulated annealing, so we can't honestly claim quantum is winning here yet. I'd suggest language like 'we showed that adding depth to our QAOA circuit meaningfully improves solution quality on a small benchmark — a promising result we're continuing to build on,' which is still a genuinely positive thing to announce, just accurate. I'd frame this as protecting the team, not undercutting them — if someone technical reads 'quantum breakthrough' and immediately sees it's a 4-node toy problem with no classical comparison, that's a much worse outcome for the team's credibility than announcing the accurate, still-positive version in the first place.
questions.example: Overclaim: 'Our team achieved a quantum breakthrough in portfolio optimization.' Honest alternative: 'Our team demonstrated that increasing QAOA circuit depth substantially improves solution quality on a benchmark optimization problem, a promising result we're now scaling up and benchmarking against classical methods.'
commonMistakes: Staying silent to avoid conflict, letting an overclaimed announcement go out
Framing the pushback as purely critical without first crediting the real, genuine result
Not proposing specific, concrete alternative language, leaving the manager without an easy path to correct course
keyPoints: Credit the genuine result first before raising concerns about the framing
Specifically name what's missing: realistic problem scale, and a benchmarked classical comparison
Propose concrete alternative language rather than only raising an objection
Frame the correction as protecting the team's credibility, not undermining their work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes crediting the genuine result before raising concerns
Correctly identifies the specific gaps between the result and a 'breakthrough' claim
Proposes concrete, honest alternative language
Frames the conversation constructively, protecting team credibility

questions.title: Disagreeing With a Teammate Who Wants to Skip the Simulator-First Development Step
questions.prompt: A teammate wants to start developing a new VQE loop directly against real IonQ hardware, arguing 'I want to see it actually run on a real QPU from day one.' You know this risks a cost like the course's $77,265 example for a 150-iteration run. How would you have this conversation, and what middle ground, if any, would you propose?
questions.modelAnswer: I would acknowledge the genuine appeal of the teammate's instinct — seeing something run on real hardware is motivating and does eventually matter — before explaining the specific cost risk concretely rather than just asserting a rule. I'd walk through the math: an 8-parameter circuit using parameter-shift gradients needs 17 circuit evaluations per iteration; 150 iterations is 2,550 evaluations; at 1,000 shots on IonQ Aria pricing, that's $77,265 for one complete run, and a typical early-development cycle involves running a half-finished, buggy version of that loop dozens of times while fixing the cost function, optimizer config, and convergence logic — multiplying that cost many times over before anything even works correctly. I would propose a concrete middle ground rather than a flat 'no': develop and debug the entire classical loop against a free or near-free classical simulator until the optimizer, cost function, and convergence logic are all independently verified correct on toy problems with known answers, and then reserve a small, clearly-scoped number of final validation runs on real IonQ hardware specifically to confirm the verified loop behaves as expected on real noise — which still satisfies the real motivation (seeing it run on a real QPU) without paying full development-cycle costs at real-hardware prices.
questions.professionalAnswer: I get the pull here — wanting to see it actually run on real hardware from day one is a reasonable instinct, and it does matter eventually. But I'd walk through the actual numbers with them: this is an 8-parameter circuit, 17 evaluations per iteration, 150 iterations is 2,550 evaluations, and at IonQ Aria pricing that's over $77,000 for one complete run — and a normal development cycle isn't one clean run, it's dozens of buggy attempts while we fix the cost function and the optimizer. I wouldn't just say no, though — I'd propose: let's debug the whole loop against a free simulator until we're confident the optimizer, the cost function, and the convergence logic are all correct on toy problems we already know the answer to, and then we run a small number of final validation runs on real hardware to confirm it behaves the way we expect with real noise. That gets them the real-hardware moment they want, just not as the place we debug from scratch.

Making an abstract argument ('it's expensive') instead of walking through the specific, concrete cost numbers
Proposing an all-or-nothing rule instead of a middle ground that still includes real-hardware validation

questions.title: Translating a Vague Resume Line Into a Specific, Hireable One
questions.prompt: A classmate's resume says 'Worked on quantum algorithms and did some research.' Using the standard of naming the specific technique, result, and tools, rewrite this into a specific resume bullet, and explain why the specific version does more work in a job search than the vague one.
questions.modelAnswer: A specific rewrite grounded in real course work might read: 'Implemented Grover's algorithm and the quantum Fourier transform in Qiskit; reproduced a published zero-noise-extrapolation result on IBM Quantum hardware across two qubit counts, diagnosing and reporting a hardware-calibration confound in the initial run; produced a full technical report and both technical and general-audience presentations.' This single bullet names the specific techniques (Grover's, QFT, zero-noise extrapolation), the specific tools (Qiskit, IBM Quantum hardware), and a specific, substantive result (identifying a real confound, not just 'got a result') — compared to 'worked on quantum algorithms and did some research,' which tells a recruiter or technical interviewer nothing they can verify, probe, or distinguish from someone who watched a few YouTube videos. The specific version does more work because it survives both a recruiter's fast skim (keywords like Qiskit, Grover's, IBM Quantum hardware are exactly what an ATS or a skimming recruiter is scanning for) and a technical interviewer's scrutiny (a specific claim like 'diagnosed a calibration confound' invites a concrete follow-up question the candidate can actually answer in depth, demonstrating real understanding rather than exposing that the vague version was covering for shallow work).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd turn it into something like: 'Implemented Grover's algorithm and the quantum Fourier transform in Qiskit; reproduced a published zero-noise-extrapolation result on IBM Quantum hardware across two qubit counts, including diagnosing a real hardware-calibration confound in the initial run; wrote up a full technical report and gave both a technical and a general-audience presentation on it.' That names actual techniques, actual tools, and an actual, specific, non-trivial result. The vague original tells a recruiter or an interviewer nothing they can act on — they can't tell if 'some research' means a semester-long project or an afternoon of reading. The specific version works on two fronts: it has the exact keywords a recruiter skim or an ATS is actually looking for, and it sets up a concrete follow-up question an interviewer can ask — 'tell me about that calibration confound' — that the candidate can actually answer in depth, which is worth far more than a vague line that would collapse under two seconds of follow-up questioning.
questions.example: Vague: 'Worked on quantum algorithms and did some research.' Specific: 'Reproduced a published zero-noise-extrapolation result on IBM Quantum hardware across two qubit counts; diagnosed and corrected for a hardware-calibration confound in the initial run.'

Not including a specific, demonstrable result (a confound diagnosed, a technique implemented) distinct from just 'did research'
Underestimating how much a specific bullet invites verifiable follow-up questions in an interview, which works in the candidate's favor

A specific bullet survives both a recruiter's keyword skim and a technical interviewer's follow-up questions

questions.title: Responding to a Vendor's Quantum Kernel Advantage Claim
questions.prompt: A vendor's marketing material claims their quantum kernel method gives a 'provable advantage' over classical SVMs for a real-world dataset your company is considering using. You know some quantum kernel constructions have proven classical hardness for contrived problems, but no demonstrated case beats a well-tuned classical kernel on real datasets. How would you communicate your concerns to your team's decision-makers?
questions.modelAnswer: I would separate the vendor's claim into the part that's true and the part that's doing unjustified work, and communicate that distinction clearly rather than either dismissing the vendor outright or accepting the claim at face value. The true part: specific quantum kernel constructions do have proven classical hardness results — but critically, these proofs apply to certain contrived, specially-constructed problems designed to demonstrate the hardness result, not to real-world datasets in general. The unjustified leap: 'provable advantage' language, applied to this specific real-world dataset, implies the advantage has been demonstrated for this use case, when in fact there is no demonstrated case in the literature where a quantum kernel's SVM beats a well-tuned classical kernel's SVM (RBF, polynomial) on accuracy or any other practically relevant measure for a real dataset — and some natural quantum kernel constructions have even been shown to suffer kernel concentration, a failure mode where kernel values cluster near a constant as qubit count grows, losing discriminative power, a kernel-method cousin of the barren plateau problem. I would recommend to decision-makers that before committing budget based on this claim, we ask the vendor directly: can you show a benchmarked result on our specific type of dataset (or a comparable public one) where your quantum kernel's SVM actually outperforms a well-tuned classical kernel's SVM, using the same fair-benchmarking standard (same instance, same success criterion, full pipeline timed) — and if they cannot produce this, the 'provable advantage' language should be treated as referring to a different, narrower mathematical result than what's being implied for our use case.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split the vendor's claim in two: the part that's actually true, and the part that's doing more work than it should. It is true that some specific quantum kernel constructions have proven hardness results — but those proofs are for particular, deliberately constructed problems built to show the hardness result, not for real-world data in general. The leap I'd flag is 'provable advantage' being applied to our actual dataset, when there's no demonstrated case anywhere in the literature of a quantum kernel's SVM beating a well-tuned classical kernel on real data — and some quantum kernels actually get worse as you add qubits, a phenomenon called kernel concentration. What I'd tell the decision-makers is: before we commit budget on this, let's ask the vendor directly to show us a fair, benchmarked comparison on our actual kind of data, not just cite the theoretical hardness result — and if they can't produce that, we should treat 'provable advantage' as referring to a narrower mathematical claim than what the marketing language implies for our situation.
questions.example: True claim: 'specific quantum kernel constructions have proven classical hardness for certain contrived problems.' Unsupported leap: 'this proves a provable advantage for your real-world dataset' — no demonstrated real-dataset case currently supports this.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the vendor's claim entirely as marketing hype without acknowledging the real, narrower theoretical result
Accepting 'provable advantage' language at face value without checking what it actually applies to
Not proposing a concrete next step (asking for a fair, benchmarked real-dataset comparison) before the decision is made
keyPoints: Proven classical hardness results exist for specific, contrived problems, not real-world datasets generally
No demonstrated case shows a quantum kernel's SVM beating a well-tuned classical kernel on real data
Kernel concentration is a documented failure mode as qubit count grows
Recommend requiring a fair, benchmarked real-dataset comparison before committing budget

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the true, narrow hardness result from the broader implied claim
Correctly notes the absence of demonstrated real-dataset advantage and kernel concentration risk
Proposes a concrete, actionable next step before committing budget
Clear, professional communication to decision-makers

questions.title: Explaining a Cost Overrun to Stakeholders After a VQE Run
questions.prompt: A VQE run you executed cost $77,265 instead of the expected $30,906, because the optimizer ran all 150 iterations instead of converging around iteration 60 as the team had hoped. Describe how you would communicate this to stakeholders, and what specific process change you would propose going forward.
questions.modelAnswer: I would communicate this transparently and specifically, leading with the concrete numbers rather than vague language: the run cost $77,265, against an expected $30,906 if convergence had occurred around iteration 60 as hoped, because the optimizer did not actually converge early and ran the full 150-iteration budget instead. I would be clear this was not a hidden or surprising cost in the sense of 'something went wrong unexpectedly' — the $77,265 figure is exactly what 150 iterations at this parameter count and shot count was always going to cost if convergence didn't happen early, which was a known possibility, not a new discovery. I would propose a concrete process change: implement an in-loop cost circuit breaker that halts the run and alerts the team once cumulative spend crosses a pre-set ceiling (e.g. $40,000, comfortably above the hoped-for $30,906 but well below the full $77,265), independent of the iteration-count cap — so that if a future run fails to converge early again, we catch and can decide whether to continue spending partway through, rather than discovering the full cost only after the run has already completed. I would also propose that initial cost estimates presented to stakeholders include both the hoped-for-convergence figure and the full-budget worst-case figure side by side, so the possibility of this exact outcome is visible and expected in advance rather than looking like a surprise after the fact.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lead with the actual numbers: we expected around $30,906 if the optimizer converged near iteration 60, but it ran the full 150 iterations instead, bringing the real cost to $77,265. I'd be clear that this isn't some mysterious overrun — $77,265 is exactly what the full iteration budget was always going to cost if early convergence didn't happen, which was a real possibility going in, not a new surprise. Going forward, I'd propose we add a cost circuit breaker inside the loop itself — something like a $40,000 ceiling that halts the run and alerts us if we're not converging as hoped, so we get a chance to make a call partway through instead of only finding out the full cost after the run is already done. And I'd propose that any future cost estimate we show stakeholders includes both numbers side by side — the hoped-for-convergence estimate and the full-budget worst case — so this exact outcome is something everyone already expected as a possibility, not a surprise after the fact.
questions.example: Cost estimate given to stakeholders going forward: 'Expected cost if convergence occurs near iteration 60: ~$30,906. Worst-case cost if full 150-iteration budget is used: $77,265. We will halt and alert at $40,000 if convergence hasn't occurred by then.'
commonMistakes: Communicating the overrun vaguely without the specific numbers
Framing the overrun as a surprising failure rather than a known possible outcome that should have been presented upfront as a range
Proposing no concrete process change, leaving the same risk to recur on the next run
keyPoints: Lead with specific numbers: $77,265 actual vs. $30,906 hoped-for-convergence estimate
Frame this as a known possible outcome, not a mysterious failure
Propose an in-loop cost circuit breaker with a pre-set alert ceiling
Propose presenting both the hoped-for and worst-case cost estimates to stakeholders upfront in the future

questions.title: Writing an Honest Limitations Section Under Pressure to Overstate Results
questions.prompt: Your capstone's quantum optimization result on a 4-node Max-Cut graph (approximation ratio 0.9999 at p=2) is genuinely strong, and a program coordinator suggests you drop the limitations section's note about problem-size scale so the report 'reads more impressively' for an upcoming showcase. How would you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: I would decline to drop the limitations note, but I would explain why clearly and constructively rather than simply refusing. The core issue is that omitting the problem-size caveat doesn't make the result more impressive — it makes it misleading, because a reader (especially a technically literate one at a showcase) who doesn't see that caveat stated explicitly may reasonably assume the 0.9999 ratio generalizes to realistically-sized problems, which hasn't been tested and, per the course's own cherry-picked-instance failure mode, would be a textbook case of presenting a small, favorable result as if it demonstrated something at scale. I would propose a middle path that serves both the coordinator's goal and research integrity: keep the genuinely strong 0.9999 result front and center as the headline, since it IS a real and interesting result, but state the scale caveat in one clear, confident sentence rather than hedging it into obscurity — something like 'This result, demonstrated on a 4-node benchmark problem, shows QAOA depth scaling can achieve near-optimal performance; we are now extending this testing to larger problem sizes.' This reads as a strong, honest result with a clear next step, not a weaker result, and it protects both my own and the program's credibility if anyone in the audience asks a pointed follow-up question about scale.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't drop it, but I also wouldn't just say no and leave it there — I'd explain why removing it actually hurts us rather than helping. The 0.9999 number is already a genuinely strong, real result; the scale caveat doesn't weaken it, it just tells people honestly what it is and isn't evidence of yet. If we drop that caveat and someone at the showcase asks 'does this hold at realistic portfolio sizes,' we're caught either admitting it on the spot looking unprepared, or worse, implying something we can't back up. What I'd propose instead is keeping the strong result as the headline and stating the caveat as one confident, forward-looking sentence — something like 'on this benchmark problem, we hit near-optimal performance, and we're now extending the testing to larger sizes' — which honestly reads as a strong result with a clear next step, not a weaker one.
questions.example: Dropped caveat version, risked question at showcase: 'Does this hold for a real 500-asset portfolio?' -> no good answer prepared. Kept-caveat version: 'On this 4-node benchmark, we demonstrated near-optimal performance; we're now extending to larger problem sizes' -> already answers the question before it's asked.
commonMistakes: Complying with the suggestion to drop the caveat to avoid conflict with the program coordinator
Refusing bluntly without explaining why the caveat actually protects the result's credibility
Not proposing a concrete alternative that keeps the strong result prominent while stating the caveat honestly
keyPoints: Omitting the scale caveat would misleadingly imply a result not actually demonstrated
The caveat doesn't weaken the genuinely strong result if stated confidently rather than hedged
Propose a specific alternative phrasing that keeps the result prominent and the caveat honest
Framing: honesty here protects credibility rather than undermining the showcase's impact

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Declines to drop the limitations note while explaining why constructively
Correctly identifies why omitting it would be misleading, not just 'less impressive'
Proposes a concrete alternative phrasing that keeps the result strong and honest

questions.title: Handling a Disagreement Over Whether a Benchmark Result Is Publishable
questions.prompt: A teammate wants to submit a paper claiming your QAOA implementation 'found a better Max-Cut solution than classical search in fewer iterations,' but you know the classical baseline used was an unoptimized greedy search, not simulated annealing or a tuned solver. How would you raise this disagreement with your teammate before submission?
questions.modelAnswer: I would raise this directly and early, framing it as protecting the paper's credibility through peer review rather than as doubting the teammate's work. I would explain specifically: comparing against an unoptimized greedy search is exactly the weak-baseline failure mode the field's own fair-benchmarking standards flag, because a quantum method can look impressive purely by beating a strawman, and any competent reviewer or reader familiar with classical optimization will immediately ask 'why didn't you compare against simulated annealing or a tuned commercial solver, the actual best classical method reasonably available for this problem class?' — a question the paper as currently framed has no good answer to. I would propose, rather than abandoning the result, that we re-run the comparison against a genuinely strong classical baseline (simulated annealing at minimum) before submission; if QAOA still shows an advantage against that stronger baseline, the paper becomes significantly more defensible and interesting; if it doesn't, that's also a legitimate, honestly-reportable finding (e.g. 'QAOA matches but does not exceed a well-tuned classical baseline at this problem size'), which protects both of our names from a weak-baseline criticism surfacing publicly after submission rather than being caught and fixed beforehand.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd bring this up early and directly, not as second-guessing their work but as trying to get ahead of exactly the criticism a reviewer is going to raise. Comparing against unoptimized greedy search is a known weak-baseline problem — any reviewer who knows classical optimization is going to ask why we didn't compare against simulated annealing or a tuned solver instead, and right now we don't have a good answer to that. What I'd propose isn't dropping the result, it's strengthening it: let's re-run the comparison against a real classical baseline before we submit. If QAOA still wins against that, we have a much more defensible, more interesting paper. If it doesn't, that's still a legitimate finding worth reporting honestly — and either way, we're catching this ourselves instead of having a reviewer catch it for us after submission.
questions.example: Current claim: 'QAOA beat classical search in fewer iterations' (baseline: unoptimized greedy). Proposed re-test: 'QAOA vs. simulated annealing, same instance, same success criterion' — a stronger, more defensible comparison either way the result comes out.

Framing the concern as a personal criticism of the teammate rather than a methodological gap
Proposing to abandon the result entirely instead of proposing a concrete path to strengthen it

questions.title: Explaining a Delayed Deliverable Caused by Underestimated Queue Time
questions.prompt: Your capstone's experimental phase is running two weeks behind schedule because real cloud quantum hardware queue times turned out to be far longer than planned, and you needed several debugging re-submissions. How would you communicate this delay to your course instructor or program coordinator, and what would you do differently next time you scope a similar project?
questions.modelAnswer: I would communicate this proactively and specifically rather than waiting to be asked, explaining the actual mechanism behind the delay rather than a vague 'it took longer than expected.' I would explain: queue time on real cloud quantum hardware, separate from actual compute time, can mean minutes to hours of wait per job submission depending on device demand, and because debugging a hybrid loop realistically takes multiple submission rounds (fixing the cost function, the optimizer config, and the convergence logic iteratively) rather than one clean submission, the cumulative queue-wait time compounded far beyond my original estimate, which treated queue time as a minor, fixed cost rather than its own significant line item. I would present a concrete, revised timeline for the remaining work rather than just explaining the delay and leaving it open-ended. Going forward, I would specifically budget queue time as its own explicit line item separate from compute time in any future project plan, estimate the realistic number of debugging iteration rounds in advance (two or three passes, not one clean pass, as the course's own capstone-scoping guidance recommends) rather than assuming the first submission would work, and build a pre-committed cut list into the original schedule so that if a delay like this one occurred again, there would already be a clear, previously agreed-upon plan for what to simplify or drop rather than needing to renegotiate scope under time pressure after the fact.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd flag this proactively, not wait for someone to ask why I'm behind, and I'd explain the actual cause specifically: queue time on real cloud hardware is its own separate cost from compute time, and because debugging a hybrid loop realistically takes several submission rounds, not one clean run, that queue-wait time added up far more than my original plan accounted for — I'd treated it as a minor detail instead of its own real line item. I'd come to that conversation with a concrete, revised plan for finishing, not just an explanation of why I'm late. Looking forward, I'd budget queue time explicitly as its own line item next time, assume two or three debugging passes rather than one clean pass, since that's the realistic pattern, and build a cut list into the schedule from day one, so if something like this happens again, there's already an agreed plan for what gets simplified instead of having to negotiate that under pressure after the fact.
questions.example: Original plan: 1 week for experimental phase, queue time treated as negligible. Actual: 3 weeks, due to 4 debugging submission rounds each waiting 1-3 hours in queue. Revised plan going forward: budget queue time explicitly (e.g. 'expect 2-4 hours of cumulative queue wait per debugging round, across an estimated 3 rounds').
